'''Anthony Danel Henry''' (born November 3, 1976) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Cleveland Browns]] in the fourth round of the [[2001 NFL draft]] and also played for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] and [[Detroit Lions]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[South Florida Bulls football|South Florida Bulls]].

==Early life==
Henry attended [[Estero High School]] in [[Estero, Florida]]. He was named the district MVP in [[track and field|track]], after setting school
records in the [[triple jump]] (44”1’) and [[high jump]] (6'6"). In football, he was named [[Lee County, Florida|Lee County]] Athlete
of the Year and district player of the year. He also lettered in [[basketball]].

==College career==
Henry accepted a scholarship from the [[University of South Florida]]. He didn't play in his first year because of failing to meet the requirements of [[Proposition 48 (NCAA)|Proposition 48]], but his work in the classroom eventually allowed the NCAA to grant him an additional year of eligibility in 2000.

As freshman he received second-team All-Independent honors at free safety after registering 73 tackles, 2 interceptions and 2 fumble recoveries. The next year, he ranked third on the team with 79 tackles and played [[quarterback]] for one series against [[Valparaiso University]]. As a junior, he started eight-of-nine games at free safety and registered 62 tackles (fourth on the team), 3 interceptions and 2 fumble recoveries. In his last year he was moved to cornerback, but also saw snaps at
free safety and wide receiver, while finishing with 40 tackles, 5 interceptions (led the team), 8 passes defensed (led the team).<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.clevelandbrowns.com/news/article-1/Pick-4-DB-Anthony-Henry/59e5f9ac-2c10-11df-8e39-01733cd36da8 |title=Pick #4: DB Anthony Henry |access-date=June 6, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307031741/http://www.clevelandbrowns.com/news/article-1/Pick-4-DB-Anthony-Henry/59e5f9ac-2c10-11df-8e39-01733cd36da8 |archive-date=March 7, 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

He was in the first batch of 4-year letter winners ever in the [[South Florida Bulls football|USF's football program]]. He ended his collegiate career with 256 tackles (9 for loss), 6 fumble recoveries, 22 passes defensed and led the team in interceptions two years in a row (1999, 2000).

Henry is a member of the [[University of South Florida Athletic Hall of Fame]] and was the Bulls first football player to be inducted into the Hall.

===Cleveland Browns===
Henry was selected by the [[Cleveland Browns]] in the fourth round of the [[2001 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2001 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2001/draft.htm |access-date=March 18, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> As a rookie, he played in 16 games (2 starts) and tied for the NFL lead in [[interceptions]] with 10. Also set a franchise record with a 97-yard interception return for a touchdown.

He saw less action his second year. In 2003, he was named the starter at right cornerback. In 2004, he tallied 76 tackles, 4 interceptions and 12 passes defensed.

During his four years with the team from 2001 to 2004, he started 39 of 61 games, recording 247 [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]], 17 interceptions,  49 passes defensed and a [[touchdown]].

===Dallas Cowboys===
Henry signed a five-year, $25 million deal with the [[Dallas Cowboys]] as an [[unrestricted free agent]] in 2005.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pasquarelli |first=Len |author-link=Len Pasquarelli |date=2005-03-03 |title=Ferguson, Henry are 'Big D'efensive additions |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/columns/story?id=2003511 |access-date=2025-07-20 |website=ESPN.com}}</ref> With a $10 million signing bonus, a $1 million roster bonus in 2005 and a $1 million roster bonus in 2006. He got paid $18 million over the first three years of his contract. He missed four games with a severe groin injury, that also limited him during the last 8 games of the year.

In 2006, he was limited with a knee injury but still recorded 90 tackles (third on the team), 23 passes defensed (led the team) and 2 interceptions. In 2007, he was limited with a high ankle sprain and still managed to lead the team with six interceptions (tied for fifth in the NFL). In 2008, he played 16 games (15 starts), registering 55 tackles (35 solo), 7 passes defensed, one interception  and 2 sacks.

On February 28, 2009, he was traded to the [[Detroit Lions]] in exchange for [[quarterback]] [[Jon Kitna]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3942507|title=Kitna sent to Cowboys; Lions acquire CB Henry|date=February 28, 2009}}</ref> He played four seasons for the Cowboys from 2005 to 2008, starting 51 of 56 games, recording 215 tackles, 12 interceptions, two [[Quarterback sack|sacks]], and two touchdowns.

===Detroit Lions===
Henry was benched in week 5 of the 2009 season because of his play and replaced with [[Phillip Buchanon]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.mlive.com/lions/index.ssf/2009/10/lions_defensive_coordinator_gu_2.html|title = Lions' starting lineup in secondary in flux|date = October 15, 2009}}</ref> He was not re-signed at the end of the year.

==Personal life==
Venturing out to Los Angeles to pursue a career in entertainment, Henry co-stars in the film ''[[Once Upon a Time in Brooklyn]]'' starring [[William DeMeo]] & [[Ice-T]]. Henry also launched his online music magazine Coool Flame (www.CooolFlame.com) in February 2013, which focused on urban music. He is also an investor with First Picks Management (owned by former NFL Player [[Keyshawn Johnson]]), owning several Panera Breads across the Southern California region.

'''Anthony Davis''' (born September 8, 1952), also known as "'''A.D.'''",<ref name=LAT112210>Lance Pugmire, [http://www.latimes.com/sports/college/usc/la-sp-anthony-davis-20101123,0,4938273.story For former USC star Anthony Davis, college football fame never translated into fortune], ''Los Angeles Times'', November 22, 2010, Accessed November 23, 2010.</ref> is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in four professional leagues: the [[World Football League]] (WFL), [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL), [[National Football League]] (NFL), and [[United States Football League]] (USFL).

Davis played [[college football]] and [[College baseball|baseball]] at the [[USC Trojans|University of Southern California]] (USC), where he was part of five national championships, two in [[USC Trojans football|football]] and three in [[USC Trojans baseball|baseball]].

==College career==
Davis was a consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] in [[1974 College Football All-America Team|1974]], and led the [[1974 USC Trojans football team|USC Trojans]] in rushing, scoring and kick return yardage for three consecutive seasons. He is especially remembered for scoring 11 [[touchdown]]s in three games against [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame]].  In a 45–23 USC win on December 2, [[1972 USC Trojans football team|1972]], he scored six touchdowns which set a school single game record. Two of those scores came on [[kickoff return]]s. He returned the opening [[Kickoff (American football)|kickoff]] 97 yards for a [[touchdown]] after Notre Dame won the [[Coin toss#Coin flipping in dispute resolution|coin toss]] and chose to kick. After Notre Dame scored on a short pass and narrowed the Trojans' lead, he returned the following [[Kickoff (American football)|kickoff]] 96 yards for a [[touchdown]]. In this game, Davis had three kickoff returns for a total of 218 yards, an average of 72.7 yards per return.<ref name=spree>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=IalVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=9-ADAAAAIBAJ&pg=2027%2C434740 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=Associated Press |title=Davis' spree leads USC to 45-23 rout |date=December 3, 1972 |page=1B}}</ref> This set an [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] record for the highest average gain per return in a single game.  In his career as a Trojan he returned 37 kickoffs for 1,299 yards, an [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] record 35.1 yard average. His six career kickoff returns for touchdowns set an NCAA record which stood until 2009, when it was broken by [[C. J. Spiller]] of [[Clemson Tigers football|Clemson]]. Davis' kickoff return average of 42.5 yards in 1974, is the highest kickoff return average for any single season leader ever.  He was also the first [[Pacific-10 Conference#Pacific-8|Pacific-8 Conference]] player to rush for more than 1,000 yards in three consecutive seasons – 1,191 in 1972; 1,112 in 1973 and 1,469 in 1974. For his career at USC, he carried the ball 784 times for 3,772 yards and 44 touchdowns.<!-- In his senior year (1974) he was a unanimous Consensus All-American selection.--> Davis was also a repeat ([[1973 All-Pacific-8 Conference football team|1973]], [[1974 All-Pacific-8 Conference football team|1974]]) first-team [[List of All-Pac-12 Conference football teams|All-Pac-8 Conference]] selection.  He was also the third multiple recipient of the [[W.J. Voit Memorial Trophy]], awarded each year to the outstanding football player on the Pacific Coast. Davis won the Voit trophy in 1972 and 1974.

On November 30, [[1974 USC Trojans football team|1974]], he started an amazing rally which brought the Trojans back from a 24–0 second quarter deficit against #4 ranked [[1974 Notre Dame Fighting Irish football team|Notre Dame]] to a 55–24 win. Just before halftime, he scored on a seven-yard [[lateral pass]] from quarterback [[Pat Haden]]. Davis found paydirt a second time on a 102-yard [[kickoff return]] to open the second half. With only 3:25 elapsed in the third quarter, Davis scored a third touchdown on a six-yard run. Then with still 8:37 left in the same quarter, Davis added his fourth and final [[touchdown]] of the game on a four-yard dash, dropped to his knees, went into his "[[Touchdown celebration|endzone dance]]", then added a [[two-point conversion]] and the Trojans had the lead 27–24. Incredibly, Davis had scored 26 of the Trojans' first 27 points.<ref name=htwodsh>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=wsdVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=PuADAAAAIBAJ&pg=3272%2C141454 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=Associated Press |title=Davis' 102-yard dash ignites SC, 55-24 |date=December 1, 1974 |page=1D}}</ref><ref name=tcqu>{{cite magazine |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1974/12/09/that-california-earthquake |magazine=Sports Illustrated |last=Jares |first=Joe |title=That California earthquake |date=December 9, 1974 |page=30}}</ref>

In [[1974 NCAA Division I football season|1974]], [[Heisman Trophy]] ballots were due prior to the end of the season and before that year's USC-Notre Dame game. He finished second in the [[1974 NCAA Division I football season#Heisman Trophy|voting]] to [[Archie Griffin]] of [[1974 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State]]. Afterward, Heisman voting took place after all the regular season games had been played. From 1972 to 1974, with Davis as the [[Halfback (American football)|tailback]] the Trojans compiled a {{winpct|31|3|2|record=y}} record, three conference titles, two [[Rose Bowl (game)|Rose Bowl]] victories in three appearances and two [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national championships]]. He accumulated 24 school, conference, and NCAA records, including over 5,400 [[all-purpose yards]] and 52 touchdowns.

Davis' talents were not just limited to football, he was also successful in [[baseball]] as an [[outfielder]] and switch-hitter on USC's [[1972 USC Trojans baseball team|1972]], [[1973 USC Trojans baseball team|1973]], and [[1974 USC Trojans baseball team|1974]] [[College World Series]] champion baseball teams.<ref name=LAT112210/> Playing with wood bats at the time, Davis hit .273 with six [[home run]]s, 45 [[Run batted in|RBIs]] and 13 [[stolen base]]s for the Trojans' 1974 team.

During his Trojan career, Davis won five national championships – two in football, three in baseball.<ref name=LAT112210/> As a two-sport standout, Davis holds the distinction of being the only player in school history to start for a national champion football team (1972) and a national champion baseball team (1974). He did not finish his degree at USC.<ref name=LAT112210/>

The Notre Dame vs. USC game on November 27, [[2004 USC Trojans football team|2004]] was titled "Anthony Davis Day", in recognition of the 30th anniversary of the record-breaking game.

While at USC, Davis was on the cover of ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' magazine three times, including one foldout.<ref name=tcqu/><ref name=unbuim>{{cite magazine |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1973/10/01/undefeated-but-improving |magazine=Sports Illustrated |title=Undefeated but improving |last=Underwood |first=John |date=October 1, 1973 |page=22}}</ref><ref name=twasag>{{cite magazine |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1973/11/05/twas-a-great-day-for-the-irish |magazine=Sports Illustrated |title='Twas a great day for the Irish |last=Putnam |first=Pat |date=November 5, 1973 |page=30}}</ref> He was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in<!--December 6,--> late 2005 in New York City, and enshrined on August 12, 2006, in [[South Bend, Indiana]].

==Professional career==
The [[1975 Minnesota Twins season|Minnesota Twins]] selected him in the fourth round of the [[Major League Baseball Draft|1975 January amateur entry draft]] (83rd overall pick) for [[Major League Baseball]] (MLB); however he rejected them, thinking they would be unable to meet his salary demands.<ref name=LAT112210/>

===World Football League===
Davis was selected by the [[1975 New York Jets season|New York Jets]] in the [[1975 NFL draft#Round two|second round]] of the [[1975 NFL draft]], 37th overall.  At the time, the Jets had veteran quarterback [[Joe Namath]] and offered a major stage, but the team's management were not willing to give in to his contract demands.<ref name=LAT112210/>  In [[1975 World Football League season|1975]], Davis opted to play for the [[Southern California Sun]] of the upstart [[World Football League]] (WFL); he signed a five-year, $1.7-million deal that reportedly included a $200,000 cash bonus and a [[List of Rolls-Royce motor cars|Rolls-Royce]].<ref name=LAT112210/>

He led the WFL in rushing with 1,200 yards on 239 carries and 16 touchdowns at the time of its demise. He also caught 40 passes for 381 yards and one touchdown, while on kickoff returns he ran back 9 for 235 yards and one touchdown. In all, he scored 18 TDs in the WFL for 133 points. His 16 touchdowns for rushing over 12 games is a WFL record. He also threw the ball and completed four of eleven attempts for 102 yards and a touchdown. The league folded during the season in October,<ref name=itovr>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=KNZVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=JuADAAAAIBAJ&pg=6366%2C6777086 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=Associated Press |title='It's over' for WFL |date=October 22, 1975 |page=1E}}</ref><ref name=cllps>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=zPJLAAAAIBAJ&sjid=ce0DAAAAIBAJ&pg=7184%2C3119091 |work=Spokesman-Review |location=Spokane, Washington |agency=Associated Press |title=World Football League collapses in hopeless debt |date=October 23, 1975 |page=34}}</ref><ref name=gossp>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=PW5YAAAAIBAJ&sjid=3fcDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6886%2C3074951 |work=The Bulletin  |location=Bend, Oregon |agency=Associated Press |title=Ghost of season past kills WFL |date=October 23, 1975 |page=13}}</ref> and Davis moved on.

===Canadian Football League===
Davis headed to the [[Canadian Football League]] in [[1976 CFL season|1976]], and became the league's first "million dollar man." His time with the [[1976 Toronto Argonauts season|Toronto Argonauts]] was not happy; his star ego clashed with CFL legend and Argos' head coach [[Russ Jackson]]'s idea of a team player as a receiver. He rushed 104 times for 417 yards, caught 37 passes for 408 yards, and scored four touchdowns; Davis later stated that his heart wasn't in it with playing for the Argonauts.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lynch |first=John |date=1990-07-14 |title=WHERE ARE THEY NOW?: ANTHONY DAVIS : A.D.'s Past Always Present : Notre Dame Nemesis Treasures Long Run as USC, Valley Legend |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-07-14-sp-271-story.html |access-date=2024-01-24 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref>

During the final regular season game against the [[1976 Hamilton Tiger-Cats season|Hamilton Tiger-Cats]] (in [[Hamilton, Ontario]]), Argonauts [[quarterback]] [[Matthew Reed]], desperate to find an open receiver, threw an [[incomplete pass]] to Davis. When Reed returned to the bench, assistant coach [[Joe Moss]] told him never to throw the ball to Davis again; he had one carry and called himself the most expensive passing decoy in football.<ref name=awhtmtf>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=qD9VAAAAIBAJ&sjid=VT4NAAAAIBAJ&pg=4252%2C2140688 |work=The Leader-Post |location=Regina, Saskatchewan|agency=Canadian Press |last=Campbell |first=Neil |title=Argos work hard to maintain tradition |date=November 8, 1976 |page=16}}</ref>

===National Football League===
The [[1977 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] had acquired the NFL rights to Davis in the [[1976 NFL expansion draft]], with his old USC head coach [[John McKay (American football)|John McKay]] hoping to turn some new magic, but Davis' NFL career was a disappointment. Tampa Bay had lost all fourteen games in [[1976 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|1976]], and injuries to the Bucs' top two quarterbacks in the [[1977 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season#Preseason|preseason]] put extra pressure on the offense. In eleven games for the Bucs in [[1977 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|1977]], he rushed 95 times for 297 yards (3.1 yard average), caught eight passes, and scored a touchdown.

In {{nfly|1978}}, Davis played two games for the [[1978 Houston Oilers season|Houston Oilers]], where he broke his leg in the same spot twice in one season. He later played two games for the [[1978 Los Angeles Rams season|Los Angeles Rams]], where he rushed three times for seven yards.

===United States Football League===
In the spring of [[1983 USFL season|1983]] at age thirty, over four years after he last played with the Rams, Davis had a short stint with the [[Los Angeles Express (USFL)|Los Angeles Express]] of the new [[1983 USFL season|USFL]], rushing twelve times for 32 yards.

==Personal life==
Following his football career, Davis found initial success as a [[real estate developer]] in the 1980s and early 1990s, while also occasionally acting in minor film and television roles.<ref name=LAT112210/>

In 1990, Davis fulfilled a long-time dream and started playing professional baseball in the short-lived [[Senior Professional Baseball Association]], playing as an [[outfielder]] for the [[San Bernardino Pride]] club.<ref>[http://www.tradingcarddb.com/Gallery.cfm/sid/10076/1991-Pacific-Senior-League?PageIndex=10 1990 San Bernardino Pride]. ''The Trading Card Database''. Retrieved on March 7, 2016.</ref> The Pride had a record of 13–12 and were in third place when the league canceled the season on December 26, less than the halfway point in a planned 56-game schedule.<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1990/12/27/sports/baseball-senior-baseball-season-canceled.html Baseball: Senior Baseball Season Canceled]. ''New York Times''. Retrieved on March 8, 2016.</ref>

In 2020, he was featured in the documentary "Quiet Explosions: Healing the Brain" produced and directed by [[Jerri Sher]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=QUIET EXPLOSIONS opens exclusively at the Laemmle in Glendale, CA Oct. 8-14 – Jewish News and Israel news – Breaking News |url=https://jewishnews.com/2021/10/08/quiet-explosions-opens-exclusively-at-the-laemmle-in-glendale-ca-oct-8-14/ |access-date=2022-04-08 |website=jewishnews.com}}</ref> The film discusses [[Chronic traumatic encephalopathy|CTE]], a degenerative brain disease from repetitive brain trauma that Davis suffers from.<ref>{{Cite web |title='Quiet Explosions' at SpIFF features Rypien, Spokane {{!}} The Spokesman-Review |url=https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2020/feb/28/quiet-explosions-at-spiff-features-rypien-spokane/ |access-date=2022-04-08 |website=www.spokesman.com|date=February 28, 2020 }}</ref>

'''Anthony George Clement''' (born April 10, 1976) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Louisiana–Lafayette Ragin' Cajuns football|Louisiana-Lafayette Ragin' Cajuns]] and was selected by the [[Arizona Cardinals]] in the second round of the [[1998 NFL draft]].

Clement also played for the [[San Francisco 49ers]] and [[New York Jets]].

==Early life==
Clement attended [[Cecilia High School]] in [[Cecilia, Louisiana|Cecilia]], [[Louisiana]], and was a [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in [[High school football|football]] and [[Track and field|track & field]]. In football, he was a [[Starting lineup|starting]] [[defensive tackle]] and won All-District 6A honors, and All-Louisiana Class AAA honors.

==College career==
Clement attended the [[University of Louisiana at Lafayette]].

==Professional career==

===Arizona Cardinals===
Clement was selected by the [[Arizona Cardinals]] in the second round (36th overall) of the [[1998 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1998 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1998/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played for the Cardinals until the 2004 season when he was released.

===San Francisco 49ers===
He signed with the [[San Francisco 49ers]] but only played one season for them in 2005.  He started just 6 games.

===New York Jets===
Clement was then signed by the [[New York Jets]] and played two seasons for them, in which he started every game. After the 2007 season Clement was released by the Jets.

===New England Patriots===
On July 21, Clement was signed by the [[New England Patriots]].  He was placed on [[injured reserve]] on August 3, 2008, and released from IR on September 10, 2008.<ref>{{Citation |date=December 26, 2011 |title=Anthony Clement - New England Patriots - 2011 Player Profile - Rotoworld.com |url=http://www.rotoworld.com/player/nfl/2060/anthony-clement}}</ref>

'''Anthony Hume Dilweg''' (born March 28, 1965) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] with the [[Green Bay Packers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1989 to 1990. Dilweg attended [[Walt Whitman High School (Bethesda, Maryland)|Walt Whitman High School]] in [[Bethesda, Maryland]], graduating in the class of 1984. He played [[college football]] for the [[Duke Blue Devils football|Duke Blue Devils]]. Dilweg was selected by Green Bay in the third round of the [[1989 NFL draft]].

==College career==
Anthony graduated from [[Duke University]] in 1989. While attending Duke, he played under coach [[Steve Spurrier]] and was named the 1988 [[Atlantic Coast Conference|ACC]] Football Player of the Year and the offensive MVP of the 1989 [[Hula Bowl]]. Dilweg holds the Duke single season record for passing yards with 3,824 in the 1988 season.<ref name="DU">{{cite web |last1=staff |title=Anthony Dilweg (2022) - Duke Athletics Hall of Fame |url=https://goduke.com/honors/duke-athletics-hall-of-fame/anthony-dilweg/153 |website=Duke University |access-date=13 December 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

Dilweg became a member of the Duke University Athletics Hall of Fame in 2022.<ref name="DU"/>

'''Anthony Joseph Fasano''' (born April 20, 1984) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Dallas Cowboys]] in the second round of the [[2006 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame Fighting Irish]]. Fasano also played for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]], [[Tennessee Titans]], and [[Miami Dolphins]].

==Early life==
Fasano attended and played [[high school football]] at [[Verona High School (New Jersey)|Verona High School]] in [[Verona, New Jersey]], where he was a four-year [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] as a [[tight end]] and [[defensive lineman]].<ref name="NotreDameBio">{{Cite web |title=Player Bio: Anthony Fasano |url=http://und.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/fasano_anthony00.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080610120907/http://und.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/fasano_anthony00.html |archive-date=June 10, 2008 |access-date=July 8, 2008 |website=UND.com}}</ref>  During his senior season in 2001, he caught 178 passes for 3,460 yards and 47 touchdowns as a tight end while also adding 219 solo tackles as a senior.<ref name="NotreDameBio" />  He set both season and career touchdown receptions records for the county (47 and 182, respectively).<ref name="NotreDameBio" />  He also set school records in receptions in a season and career, touchdowns in a season and solo tackles in a season.<ref name="NotreDameBio" />  Fasano finished his career with 668 catches and more than 8,500 yards and played in the [[U.S. Army All-American Bowl]].<ref name="NotreDameBio" />

Fasano also earned eight letters in other sports, including four in [[basketball]], two in [[baseball]], and two in [[track and field|track]].<ref name="NotreDameBio" />  During his first baseball outing as a freshman, he pitched a perfect game.<ref name="NotreDameBio" />  He was a two-time all-league selection in baseball, and a two-time captain in basketball.<ref name="NotreDameBio" />

He was a two-time All-state and three-time All-conference selection in track, where he won the New Jersey Group 1 state championship in the [[javelin throw]] in his first year competing in the event, with a throw of 234 ft 1 in (71.36 m). He also threw the [[shot put]]. He also holds the record for the longest home run hit in a regular season game in Verona High School history.

Fasano was raised as a [[Roman Catholic]]. He is of [[Italian people|Italian]] heritage and speaks [[Spanish language|Spanish]] and [[Italian language|Italian]] fluently.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tennessee Titans official media guide player bio |url=http://www.titansonline.com/team/roster/Anthony-Fasano/260bf2f0-d731-4c0d-ad4a-c345e7e5fa07 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170315132847/http://www.titansonline.com/team/roster/anthony-fasano/260bf2f0-d731-4c0d-ad4a-c345e7e5fa07/ |archive-date=March 15, 2017 |website=titansonline.com}}</ref>

==College career==
As a freshman at the [[University of Notre Dame]] in 2002, Fasano failed to see playing time.<ref name="NotreDameBio" />  The following season, he appeared in 11 games while starting three.<ref name="NotreDameBio" />  He finished the season with 18 receptions for 169 yards and two touchdowns.<ref name="NotreDameBio" />  Fasano caught four passes for 33 yards, including first career touchdown on a two-yard pass from [[Brady Quinn]], against [[USC Trojans football|USC]].<ref name="NotreDameBio" /><ref name="FirstTD">{{Cite web |title=Irish Fall To No. 5 USC |url=http://und.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/recaps/101803aaa.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071207162126/http://und.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/recaps/101803aaa.html |archive-date=December 7, 2007 |access-date=July 8, 2008 |website=UND.com}}</ref>

In 2004, Fasano started nine of the 11 games in which he appeared for the Fighting Irish.<ref name="NotreDameBio" />  In a game against [[Purdue Boilermakers football|Purdue]], Fasano earned [[John Mackey (American football)|John Mackey]] National Tight End of the Week honors after catching eight passes for 155 yards (a school record).<ref name="NotreDameBio" />  In a game against [[Washington Huskies football|Washington]], Fasano caught the pass from quarterback Brady Quinn in the famous "Pass right" play.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2005 vs. Washington – Pass Right – 125 Years of Notre Dame Football – Moment #060 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jw-5DdUFw6w |website=[[YouTube]]}}</ref> He went on to catch two touchdown passes that game.<ref name="NotreDameBio" /> Fasano finished the season with 27 receptions for 367 yard and four touchdowns.<ref name="NotreDameBio" />

During his 2005 senior season, Fasano caught 47 passes for 576 yards (both third on the team) and two touchdowns.<ref name="2005Stats">{{Cite web |title=2005 Overall Individual Statistics |url=http://und.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/stats/2005-2006/teamcume.html#TEAM.IND |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080610120912/http://und.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/stats/2005-2006/teamcume.html |archive-date=June 10, 2008 |access-date=July 8, 2008 |website=UND.com}}</ref>  His touchdown catches on the season came against [[Navy Midshipmen football|Navy]] and [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee]],<ref name="NotreDameBio" /> both on passes from Brady Quinn.<ref name="NotreDameBio" />  He was one of three finalists for the [[John Mackey Award]], given annually to the nation's top tight end.<ref name="NotreDameBio" />

Fasano finished his collegiate career with 92 catches for 1,112 yards and eight touchdowns.<ref name="DolphinsBio">{{Cite web |title=TEAM: Roster Anthony Fasano Profile |url=http://www.miamidolphins.com/newsite/team/roster/playerBio.asp?docid=33140 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080813223326/http://www.miamidolphins.com/newsite/team/roster/playerBio.asp?docid=33140 |archive-date=August 13, 2008 |access-date=July 8, 2008 |website=MiamiDolphins.com}}</ref>  He left Notre Dame ranking second all-time in receptions and receiving yards by a tight end.<ref name="DolphinsBio" />

Fasano did not run the 40-yard dash at the [[NFL Scouting Combine]] in February 2006 due to an injured hamstring.<ref name="KFFL" /> However, at Notre Dame's Pro Day in March, Fasano posted 40-yard dash times of 4.74 and 4.71 seconds.<ref name="KFFL" />

Prior to the [[2006 NFL draft]], Fasano visited with the [[Dallas Cowboys]], [[New York Jets]], [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], and [[Washington Redskins]].<ref name="KFFL" />

===Dallas Cowboys===
====2006 season====
Despite the presence of [[All-Pro]] [[tight end]] [[Jason Witten]], the [[Dallas Cowboys]] selected Fasano in the second round (53rd overall) of the [[2006 NFL draft]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=2006 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2006/draft.htm |access-date=May 9, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}}</ref> with the intent of running more two-tight end sets.<ref name="DolphinsBio" /> It was reported that Fasano reminded then-head coach [[Bill Parcells]] of former [[NFL]] tight end [[Mark Bavaro]], who played under Parcells with the [[New York Giants]].<ref name="KFFL" /> Fasano agreed to terms on a contract with the Cowboys on July 27.<ref name="DolphinsBio" />

Fasano appeared in all 16 games while starting in five of them during his rookie year.<ref name="DolphinsBio" /> He became the third rookie tight end in franchise history to start the season opener when he opened the game against the [[2006 Jacksonville Jaguars season|Jacksonville Jaguars]] on September 10.<ref name="DolphinsBio" /> Fasano finished the season with 14 catches for 126 yards, and was also part of a blocking unit that helped [[running back]] [[Julius Jones (American football)|Julius Jones]] rush for over 1,000 yards.<ref name="DolphinsBio" />

====2007 season====
A shoulder injury bothered Fasano throughout training camp and preseason in 2007,<ref name="KFFL" /> but he went on to appear in every one of the team's regular season games while starting six of them.<ref name="DolphinsBio" /> Fasano caught his first NFL touchdown on a 26-yard pass from quarterback [[Tony Romo]] against the [[2007 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]] on November 29.<ref name="DolphinsBio" /><ref name="FirstTDGame">{{Cite web |title=NFL Game Center: Post Game – Green Bay Packers at Dallas Cowboys – 2007 Week 13 |url=http://www.nfl.com/gamecenter?game_id=29371&displayPage=tab_gamecenter&season=2007&seasonType=REG&week=13 |access-date=July 8, 2008 |website=NFL.com}}</ref> He suffered a mild concussion during Week 15 but did not miss a game.<ref name="KFFL" /> Fasano finished his second professional season with 14 receptions for 143 yards and a touchdown.<ref name="DolphinsBio" />

During the 2007 season, [[Wade Phillips]] became the new Cowboys head coach and [[Jason Garrett]] was named the [[offensive coordinator]]. At the end of the year, the team decided that he was not a good fit for their offensive system. He underwent shoulder surgery in January 2008.

===Miami Dolphins (first stint)===
[[File:Anthony Fasano.jpg|thumb|Fasano in 2009]]

====2008 season====
On April 25, 2008, the [[Miami Dolphins]] agreed to acquire Fasano, along with [[linebacker]] [[Akin Ayodele]], from the Cowboys in exchange for a fourth-round pick (100th overall) in the [[2008 NFL draft]].<ref name="MiamiTrade">{{Cite web |title=Dallas Cowboys deal Ayodele, Fasano to Miami for 4th-round pick |url=http://www.dallasnews.com/sharedcontent/dws/spt/stories/042608dnspocowtrade.9d8d3c04.html |access-date=July 8, 2008 |website=DallasNews.com}}</ref> Dolphins executive vice president [[Bill Parcells]], general manager [[Jeff Ireland]], head coach [[Tony Sparano]], and other assistants were with the Cowboys organization when Fasano was selected in 2006.<ref name="MiamiTrade" /> The pick sent to Dallas for Fasano was eventually traded to the [[Oakland Raiders]], who used it to select [[cornerback]] [[Tyvon Branch]].<ref name="TyvonBranch">{{Cite web |title=Tyvon Branch |url=http://www.raiders.com/Team/PlayerBio.aspx?id=43486 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080510003314/http://www.raiders.com/Team/PlayerBio.aspx?id=43486 |archive-date=May 10, 2008 |access-date=July 8, 2008 |website=Raiders.com}}</ref>

During his first season with the Dolphins, Fasano caught 34 passes for 454 yards and a career-high seven touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anthony Fasano 2008 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FasaAn00/gamelog/2008/ |access-date=2024-12-22 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

====2009 season====
[[File:Anthony Fasano1.jpg|thumb|left|Fasano in 2009]]
In 2009, Fasano recorded 339 yards for two touchdowns as the Dolphins finished with a 7–9 record.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anthony Fasano 2009 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FasaAn00/gamelog/2009/ |access-date=2024-12-22 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=2009 Miami Dolphins Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees, Injury Reports |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/mia/2009.htm |access-date=2024-12-22 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

====2010 season====
During training camp in August, Fasano switched from #81 to #80 after fellow [[tight end]] [[Aaron Halterman]], who had previously worn #80, was waived/injured. On November 16, 2010, he signed a contract extension for two years worth up to $7.75 million. Overall, Fasano finished the 2010 season with a career-high 528 yards and 4 touchdowns as the Dolphins finished with a 7–9 record for the second consecutive year.

====2011 season====
In 2011, Fasano recorded 32 receptions 451 yards for 5 touchdowns as the Dolphins finished with a 6–10 record.

====2012 season====
In 2012, Fasano recorded a career-high 41 receptions for 332 yards and 5 touchdowns as the Dolphins finished with a 7–9 record.

===Kansas City Chiefs===
====2013 season====
Fasano signed as a [[free agent]] with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] on March 12, 2013.<ref name="f105">{{cite web | last=Gantt | first=Darin | title=Report: Chiefs agree to deal with Anthony Fasano | website=NBC Sports | date=2013-03-12 | url=https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/report-chiefs-agree-to-deal-with-anthony-fasano | access-date=2024-12-22}}</ref> A very durable player, that year he played in only nine games due to different injuries (knee, ankle, and concussion), registering 23 receptions for 200 yards and 3 touchdowns.<ref name="n259">{{cite web | last=Paylor| first=Terez A. | title=Chiefs’ Anthony Fasano gunning for a bounce-back year after an injury-plagued 2013 | website=Kansas City Star | date=2014-08-03 | url=https://www.kansascity.com/sports/nfl/kansas-city-chiefs/article984269.html | access-date=2024-12-27}}</ref>

====2014 season====
Fasano had a good start to the 2014 season, but a knee contusion limited his play after week 10 and although he remained the starter, he was phased out of the offense in favor of [[Travis Kelce]]. Fasano finished the 2014 season recording 226 yards and 4 touchdowns. He was released in a salary cap move on February 26, 2015.<ref name="a894">{{cite web | last=Teicher | first=Adam | title=Chiefs release veteran tight end Fasano | website=ESPN.com | date=2015-02-26 | url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/12387999/kansas-city-chiefs-release-vet-tight-end-anthony-fasano | access-date=2024-12-22}}</ref> In an episode of his podcast [[New Heights (podcast)|''New Heights'']], Kelce credits Fasano as a mentor who modeled the professionalism and weekly routine needed to succeed in the league.<ref>{{Cite podcast |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QdAQcCtY6GY |title=Patrick Mahomes on QB Rivals, Brady Advice & Curry Comps – New Heights w/Jason & Travis Kelce, EP 15 |website=youtube |publisher=Jukes |host=Kelce, Jason; Kelce, Travis |date=December 1, 2022 |access-date=December 1, 2022}}</ref>

===Tennessee Titans===
After his release from the Chiefs, on March 13, 2015, Fasano signed a two-year contract with the [[Tennessee Titans]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wyatt |first=Jim |title=Titans reach deal with TE Anthony Fasano, sources say |url=https://www.tennessean.com/story/titansinsider/2015/03/13/titans-anthony-fasano-chiefs/70271654/ |access-date=March 13, 2015 |publisher=The Tennessean}}</ref> In his first year with the Titans, Fasano recorded 289 yards and two touchdowns, which included the game-winner in overtime against the [[2015 New Orleans Saints season|New Orleans Saints]].

In 2016, Fasano recorded 8 receptions for 83 yards for 2 touchdowns as the Titans finished with a 9–7 record and narrowly missed the playoffs.

===Miami Dolphins (second stint)===
On March 9, 2017, Fasano signed a one-year contract with the Dolphins.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 9, 2017 |title=Press Release: Dolphins Sign Fasano |url=http://www.miamidolphins.com/news/press-releases/article-1/PRESS-RELEASE-Dolphins-Sign-Fasano/dea10baf-cd5f-43cf-9208-5ec132b7fa7d |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170505152139/http://www.miamidolphins.com/news/press-releases/article-1/PRESS-RELEASE-Dolphins-Sign-Fasano/dea10baf-cd5f-43cf-9208-5ec132b7fa7d |archive-date=May 5, 2017 |access-date=March 10, 2017 |website=MiamiDolphins.com}}</ref> He finished the season with 12 receptions for 107 yards and a touchdown.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anthony Fasano 2017 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FasaAn00/gamelog/2017/ |access-date=2024-12-22 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

'''Anthony Franklin Floyd''' (born February 1, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (football position)|safety]] for the [[Indianapolis Colts]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FloyAn20.htm|title=Anthony Floyd|work=Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|accessdate=December 5, 2009}}</ref> He played [[college football]] for the [[Louisville Cardinals football|Louisville Cardinals]]. He spent the 2006 [[NFL Europe]] season with the [[Berlin Thunder]], where he earned All-NFL Europe honors after making four [[interception]]s, tied for second in the league. He spent the 2006 NFL preseason with the [[Houston Texans]] before being released at the conclusion of training camp.

==Early life==
{{BLP unreferenced section|date=July 2014}}
Floyd attended [[Chaney High School (Youngstown, Ohio)|Chaney High School]] in [[Youngstown, Ohio]], and earned three [[varsity letters]] together in football and [[basketball]], and four in [[Track and field|track]].

U.S. from [[Cuba]] after [[Fidel Castro]] took power.[http://www.wkyc.com/news/politics/local-cuban-american-businessman-talks-presidents-trip/98804544 Local Cuban-American businessman talks President's trip]{{Dead link|date=December 2022 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} His father is president of Ferragon Corporation, a steel company. === Athletics === Gonzalez attended St. Joseph grade school in [[Avon Lake, Ohio]], and [[Saint Ignatius High School (Cleveland, Ohio)|Saint Ignatius High School]] in [[Cleveland, Ohio]], where he was a standout in both football and track. In football, he was a two-way player. As a senior, he was a first-team All-state honoree as well as the [[Associated Press]] and ''[[The Plain Dealer]]'' Co-defensive Player of the Year, catching 71 passes for 1,873 yards and scoring 21 touchdowns. His 26.4 yards per catch set a school record. In track, he lettered for four years and qualified for the state finals as a junior and senior. Gonzalez also played basketball as a freshman.{{citation needed|date=November 2017}} He attended Ohio State University and was an Academic All-American majoring in philosophy,{{cite news|publisher=Colts.com |url=http://www.colts.com/sub.cfm?page=bio&player_id=443 |title=Anthony Gonzalez: The Official Website of the Indianapolis Colts |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080905181706/http://www.colts.com/sub.cfm?page=bio&player_id=443 |archive-date=September 5, 2008 }} in which he earned a bachelor's degree. ==Football career== ===College=== Gonzalez was a three-year letterman at [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State University]], playing with fellow future NFL wide receivers [[Santonio Holmes]], [[Ted Ginn Jr.]], and [[Roy Hall (wide receiver)|Roy Hall]], as well as [[Heisman Trophy]]-winning quarterback [[Troy Smith]]. As a junior, Gonzalez was an All-Big Ten choice by league coaches. He finished his college career playing in the [[2007 BCS National Championship Game]], where the Buckeyes lost to the Florida Gators 41–14. {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" |- ! rowspan="2" | Year ! He was one of three Ohio State receivers selected in that draft.{{Cite web |title=2007 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2007/draft.htm |access-date=May 11, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} In Gonzalez's first year, he caught 37 passes for 576 yards and three touchdowns. The next season he caught 57 passes for 664 yards and four touchdowns. In 2009, Gonzalez earned the starting wide receiver position along with [[Reggie Wayne]] after [[Marvin Harrison]] was released from the team in the off-season. He injured his right knee during the season opener against [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] and was expected to miss up to eight weeks.{{cite news|work=Nfl.com|url=http://www.nfl.com/news/story?id=09000d5d812b13f4&template=with-video-with-comments&confirm=true|title=Colts WR Gonzalez could miss up to eight weeks; Baskett signs}} He failed to return that season and was placed on [[injured reserve]] on December 24. In 2010, Gonzalez lost the starting wide receiver position due to missing the 2009 season. He played in a total of two games as a slot receiver with five catches for 67 yards and no touchdowns. He injured his left leg in week eight against the Houston Texans and was placed on Injured Reserve for the rest of the year. Gonzalez's role in the Colts offense diminished even further during the 2011 season. He played in only eight games and did not catch a pass. He became an unrestricted free agent in the following off-season. During Gonzalez's time with Indianapolis, the Colts won three [[AFC South]] Division titles (2007, 2009, 2010), an [[AFC Championship]] (2009), and a trip to [[Super Bowl XLIV]]. ====New England Patriots==== On March 17, 2012, Gonzalez signed with the [[New England Patriots]].{{cite news|publisher=Patriots.com|url=http://www.patriots.com/news/article-1/Patriots-sign-free-agent-WR-Anthony-Gonzalez/bcc4f109-3b29-4f38-9a28-c8db3a94530f|title=Patriots sign free agent WR Anthony Gonzalez|access-date=March 17, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120320011047/http://www.patriots.com/news/article-1/Patriots-sign-free-agent-WR-Anthony-Gonzalez/bcc4f109-3b29-4f38-9a28-c8db3a94530f|archive-date=March 20, 2012|url-status=dead}} The Patriots released him on May 29, 2012.{{cite news|publisher=SBnation.com|url=http://boston.sbnation.com/new-england-patriots/2012/5/29/3050633/new-england-patriots-offseason-moves-2012-nfl-free-agency-anthony-gonzalez-released|title=Patriots Release WR Anthony Gonzalez}} ====Career statistics==== ===== Regular season ===== {| class=wikitable style="text-align:center;" |- ! colspan="2" |Total !2 !1 !10 !176 !17.6 !55 !1 |} ===Retirement=== Gonzalez decided to retire from sports and enrolled in the [[Stanford Graduate School of Business]] in September 2012,{{cite news|title=Ex-Indianapolis Colts receiver Anthony Gonzalez is in graduate school|url=http://www.indystar.com/article/20120928/SPORTS03/209280368/Ex-Indianapolis-Colts-receiver-Anthony-Gonzlaez-graduate-school|newspaper=Indy Star|date=September 28, 2012}} from which he received a master of business administration degree. ==U.S. House of Representatives== === Elections === ==== 2018 ==== {{see also|2018 United States House of Representatives elections in Ohio#District 16}} In 2018, Gonzalez filed to run as a Republican for the [[United States House of Representatives]] in [[Ohio's 16th congressional district]]. His predecessor, [[Jim Renacci]], was retiring to mount an unsuccessful [[2018 United States Senate election in Ohio|Senate campaign]] against incumbent [[Sherrod Brown]]. Gonzalez won the November 6 election with 57% of the vote, becoming the first Latino to represent Ohio in Congress.[http://www.cleveland.com/open/index.ssf/2017/09/anthony_gonzalez_former_ohio_s.html Anthony Gonzalez, former Ohio State University football star, files to run for Congress in Ohio][https://www.yahoo.com/sports/9-former-athletes-running-office-performed-tuesdays-election-053416828.html How the 9 former athletes running for office performed in Tuesday's election] He raised more than $525,000 in less than a month after announcing his run, including donations from former NFL teammate [[Peyton Manning]], [[Cleveland Browns]] owner [[Jimmy Haslam]], and several other former NFL and college football players.[http://www.cleveland.com/metro/index.ssf/2017/10/peyton_manning_other_sports_fi.html Peyton Manning, other sports figures get behind Anthony Gonzalez's bid for Congress]{{cite tweet |author=CuyahogaGOP |user=CuyahogaGOP |number=966046738409762816 |date=February 20, 2018 |title=2018 Endorsements https://t.co/WfHNAEYIvT |language=en |access-date=January 23, 2021}} Along with Texas Democrat [[Colin Allred]], he was one of two former NFL players to be elected to Congress in 2018. ==== 2020 ==== {{see also|2020 United States House of Representatives elections in Ohio #District 16}} Gonzalez defeated the Democratic nominee, physicist Aaron Paul Godfrey,{{cite web |last1=Eaton |first1=Sabrina |title=Christina Hagan files to challenge Tim Ryan: See who's running for Congress in Northeast Ohio |url=https://www.cleveland.com/open/2019/12/christina-hagan-files-to-challenge-tim-ryan-see-whos-running-for-congress-in-northeast-ohio.html |website=cleveland.com |access-date=February 17, 2021 |date=December 18, 2019}} 63.2% to 36.8%.{{cite web |title=2020 OFFICIAL ELECTIONS RESULTS |url=https://www.ohiosos.gov/elections/election-results-and-data/2020/ |website=Ohio Secretary of State |access-date=February 17, 2021 |archive-date=June 9, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200609033241/https://www.ohiosos.gov/elections/election-results-and-data/2020/ |url-status=dead }} ==== 2022 ==== {{see also|2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Ohio#District 16}} Gonzalez originally ran for reelection in the 16th district, prompting a primary challenge from Republicans who supported former President [[Donald Trump]] due to Gonzalez's impeachment vote.{{cite web |last1=Isenstadt |first1=Alex |title=Trump aide preps primary against Ohio impeachment supporter |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2021/02/22/trump-max-miller-ohio-470684 |website=Politico |access-date=March 1, 2021 |date=February 22, 2021}} Ohio's slow population growth in the [[2020 United States census]] made the district obsolete as of 2023, leaving the campaigns' statuses unclear.{{cite news|url=https://www.cleveland.com/open/2021/04/ohio-loses-a-congressional-seat-in-apportionment-from-census-2020-results.html|title=Ohio loses a congressional seat in apportionment from census 2020 results|publisher=The Plain Dealer|last=Exner|first=Rich|date=April 26, 2021|accessdate=April 28, 2021}} On September 16, Gonzalez announced he would not run for Congress in 2022. === Tenure === [[File:President Trump Signs H.R. 1424 - The Fallen Warrior Battlefield Cross Memorial Act (49350876498).jpg|thumb|right|Gonzalez with [[President of the United States|President]] [[Donald Trump]] in January 2020]] The House of Representatives [[First impeachment of Donald Trump|impeached]] President [[Donald Trump]] on December 18, 2019, claiming Trump had abused the power of his office and obstructed the will of Congress by seeking foreign aid to influence the results of the 2020 election against challenger [[Joe Biden]]. Gonzalez voted not to impeach Trump, saying there was not enough evidence.{{cite news | publisher = patch.com | date = December 18, 2019 | title = Strongsville Rep. Anthony Gonzalez Votes Against Impeachment Gonzalez said he didn't feel there was direct evidence tying President Donald Trump to abuses of power. | author = Chris Mosby | url = https://patch.com/ohio/strongsville/strongsville-rep-anthony-gonzalez-votes-against-impeachment }} The [[United States Senate|Senate]] voted mostly on party lines to acquit Trump of the charges on February 5, 2020.{{Cite web|title='Not Guilty': Trump Acquitted On 2 Articles Of Impeachment As Historic Trial Closes|url=https://www.npr.org/2020/02/05/801429948/not-guilty-trump-acquitted-on-2-articles-of-impeachment-as-historic-trial-closes|access-date=February 8, 2021|website=NPR.org|date=February 5, 2020|language=en|last1=Ewing|first1=Philip}} Just 12 days before the end of Trump's term, the House passed [[Second impeachment of Donald Trump|a second impeachment resolution]] with one article claiming "incitement of insurrection", before and during the [[2021 United States Capitol attack|U.S. Capitol attack]]. Gonzalez was one of ten Republicans who voted to impeach Trump for this offense.{{cite news |url=https://www.fox35orlando.com/news/10-gop-lawmakers-break-with-party-in-house-vote-to-impeach-trump |title=10 GOP lawmakers vote to impeach Trump, trial moves to Senate |work=[[WOFL|FOX 35]] |date=January 13, 2021}}{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/01/13/politics/house-republicans-vote-yes-impeachment/index.html|title=These 10 House Republicans voted to impeach Trump on Wednesday|publisher=CNN|date=January 13, 2021|access-date=January 13, 2021}}{{cite tweet |author=Rep. Anthony Gonzalez |user=RepAGonzalez |number=1349461350456717312 |date=January 13, 2021 |title=See my full statement on impeachment below. https://t.co/pBBYRI2RUP |language=en |access-date=January 23, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115100213/https://twitter.com/repagonzalez/status/1349461350456717312 |archive-date=January 15, 2021 |url-status=live}} The Senate again acquitted Trump. Ohio Republican Party chair [[Bob Paduchik]] said the second impeachment resolution addressed "an unconstitutional, politically motivated process that served no purpose." As a result of his vote to impeach Trump, the Ohio Republican Central Committee voted to censure Gonzalez, stating that Gonzalez had "betrayed his constituents" and "relied on emotions rather than the will of his constituents and any credible facts".{{cite news | publisher = thehill.com | date = May 7, 2021 | title = Ohio GOP censures Republican lawmaker over Trump | author = JORDAN WILLIAMS | url = https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/552362-ohio-gop-censures-rep-anthony-gonazlez-calls-for-resignation-over-vote}} Gonzalez and his family received continual threats following the impeachment vote, and he took additional security measures to protect his wife and family.{{cite web |last1=Martin |first1=Jonathan |title=Ohio House Republican, Calling Trump 'a Cancer,' Bows Out of 2022 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/09/16/us/politics/anthony-gonzalez-ohio-trump.html |website=The New York Times |access-date=September 17, 2021 |date=September 17, 2021}} On May 19, 2021, Gonzalez was one of 35 Republicans who joined all Democrats in voting to approve legislation to establish the [[January 6 commission]] meant to investigate the [[2021 storming of the United States Capitol|storming of the U.S. Capitol]].{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/05/19/politics/house-republicans-january-6-commission/index.html|title=Here are the 35 House Republicans who voted for the January 6 commission|publisher=CNN|last=LeBlanc|first=Paul|date=May 19, 2021|accessdate=May 19, 2021}} In retaliation, Trump endorsed former White House aide [[Max Miller (Ohio politician)|Max Miller]] in the 2022 primary for the seat.[https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/former-trump-press-secretary-stephanie-grisham-accuses-congressional-candidate-of-abuse/2021/10/05/ac8617e2-25fb-11ec-8831-a31e7b3de188_story.html Former Trump press secretary Stephanie Grisham accuses congressional candidate of abuse], ''[[Washington Post]]'', Felicia Sonmez, October 5, 2021. Retrieved October 6, 2021. On October 21, 2021, Gonzalez was one of nine House Republicans who voted to hold [[Steve Bannon]] in contempt of Congress.{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/10/21/politics/house-republicans-vote-yes-steve-bannon-contempt-of-congress/index.html|title=These are the 9 House Republicans who voted to hold Steve Bannon in contempt of Congress|website=[[CNN]]|date=October 21, 2021 }} On November 5, 2021, he was among the 13 House Republicans to break with their party and vote with a majority of Democrats in favor of the [[Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act]].{{Cite web|author=Annie Grayer|title=These 6 House Democrats voted against the infrastructure bill. These 13 Republicans voted for it.|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/11/05/politics/infrastructure-bill-house-democrats-voted-no-republicans-voted-yes/index.html|access-date=November 6, Marriage Act]], which would codify the right to same-sex marriage in federal law.{{Cite news |last=Lai |first=Stephanie |date=July 19, 2022 |title=House Passes Same-Sex Marriage Bill Amid Concern About Court Reversal |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/07/19/us/politics/house-gay-marriage-bill.html |access-date=July 19, 2022 |issn=0362-4331}} ==== '''Anthony La'Ron Hargrove''' (born July 20, 1983) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[St. Louis Rams]] in the third round of the [[2004 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football|Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets]].

Hargrove also played for the [[Buffalo Bills]] as well as winning [[Super Bowl XLIV]] with the [[New Orleans Saints]], beating [[Peyton Manning]] and the [[Indianapolis Colts]]. He was also a member of the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] and [[Seattle Seahawks]] in 2011, and [[Green Bay Packers]] in 2012.

==Early life==
Hargrove played [[high school football]] at [[Port Charlotte High School]] in Florida. He played [[quarterback]] and [[free safety]] for the Pirates, before moving to defensive line in college.

==College career==
Hargrove started 13 of 24 games for the [[Georgia Tech]] Yellow Jackets, with 70 tackles (36 solo) with six sacks, 19 tackles for loss, two forced fumbles, two fumble recoveries, and three passes defensed.  He was academically ineligible for the season as a junior in 2003, but started every game at weakside defensive end as a sophomore.

==Professional career==
===St. Louis Rams===
Hargrove was selected in the third round (91st overall) by the [[St. Louis Rams]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |title=2004 NFL Draft Listing |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2023-05-06}}</ref>  On July 24, 2004, Hargrove signed a three-year $1.25 million contract with the Rams, including a signing bonus of $442,000. As a reserve in 2004, Hargrove played in 15 games and started two. He totaled 31 tackles (23 solo) and recorded one sack. In 2005, he was the Rams starting right defensive end, totaling 51 tackles (43 solo) and 6.5 sacks. In 2006, he played in four games with two starts and had five tackles and one-half sack. Early in the 2006 season Hargrove had an unexplained two-day absence which caused him to be made inactive and then traded.<ref>[https://www.usatoday.com/sports/football/nfl/2006-09-21-notebook_x.htm USA Today]</ref>

===Buffalo Bills===
Hargrove was traded by the Rams to the [[Buffalo Bills]] on October 16, 2006, in exchange for a fifth-round pick in the [[2007 NFL draft]]. Hargrove played in 10 games in 2006 and had 19 tackles (14 solo) and recorded a sack to make his 2006 totals 24 tackles and 1.5 sacks with both the Bills and Rams. On March 1, 2007, Hargrove signed the Bills' one-year tender of $850,000 for the 2007 season. In 2007, he played 12 games and made 28 tackles (18 solo) and had 1.5 sacks after serving a four-game suspension, which cost him $200,000 of his 2007 salary.

On August 11, 2007, Hargrove was suspended by the NFL for the first four games of the regular season for breaking the NFL's substance abuse policy.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Bills player accused of breaking cop's glasses |publisher=Atlanta Journal-Constitution |url=http://www.ajc.com/sports/content/sports/stories/2007/08/05/hargrove_0805.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120718170306/http://www.ajc.com/sports/content/sports/stories/2007/08/05/hargrove_0805.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 18, 2012 |access-date=August 5, 2007 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news| title = Bills' DE Hargrove charged with misdemeanors after altercation outside nightclub | publisher = San Diego Union Tribune/Associated Press | url = http://www.signonsandiego.com/sports/nfl/20070805-1330-fbn-bills-playerarrested.html | access-date = August 5, 2007}}</ref> It was reported on January 18, 2008, that Hargrove had failed another drug test. Due to past violations of the NFL's substance abuse policy, Hargrove received a one-year suspension on January 24, 2008.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.skysports.com/story/0,19528,12118_3068741,00.html | work=Sky Sports | title=Hargrove handed one-year ban | date=January 21, 2008}}</ref> It was announced he had been reinstated by the league on February 23, 2009.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://myespn.go.com/blogs/afceast/0-5-109/Hargrove-reinstated-by-NFL.html |title=Hargrove reinstated by NFL - AFC East - ESPN |access-date=February 23, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090226223348/http://myespn.go.com/blogs/afceast/0-5-109/Hargrove-reinstated-by-NFL.html |archive-date=February 26, 2009 }}</ref>

===New Orleans Saints===
On May 18, 2009, Hargrove signed a contract with the New Orleans Saints.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2009-05-19 |title=Saints plan ahead, sign free-agent DE Hargrove |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=4179223 |access-date=2025-08-03 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press |language=en}}</ref> New Orleans Saints defensive coordinator Gregg Williams moved Hargrove inside to defensive tackle where he flourished.<ref>Jennifer Armstrong, [http://www.nola.com/saints/index.ssf/2009/09/anthony_hargrove_has_found_hom.html "Anthony Hargrove has found home as New Orleans Saints tackle"], ''[[Times-Picayune]]'', September 3, 2009.</ref>

On November 8 of the same year Hargrove validated the Saints' decision by recovering a [[fumble]] from the [[Carolina Panthers]] and scoring a 4th-quarter touchdown, sealing a 30–20 victory for the Saints. Besides the rare occurrence of a touchdown scored by a [[defensive lineman]], the game was Panthers coach [[John Fox (American football)|John Fox]]'s first loss in the [[Louisiana Superdome]] and put New Orleans at a season-starting eight wins and no losses for the first time in Saints history.<ref name="HargroveTrip20091109pD6">{{Cite news|url=http://www.nola.com/sports/t-p/index.ssf?/base/sports-45/1257747671116120.xml&coll=1|title=Hargrove making most of his chance|last=Triplett|first=Mike|date=November 9, 2009|work=Times-Picayune|pages=D6|access-date=November 9, 2009}}</ref>

Hargrove was a [[restricted free agent]] after the 2009 season, and it was reported that the [[Detroit Lions]] were interesting in signing him, but on April 5, 2010, Hargrove signed the Saints' qualifying tender, and the Saints said he would return to the team in 2010.<ref>Sean Leahy, [http://content.usatoday.com/communities/thehuddle/post/2010/04/saints-to-bring-back-anthony-hargrove-after-dt-signs-offer-sheet/1 "Saints to bring back Anthony Hargrove after DT signs offer sheet"], ''[[USA Today]]'', April 5, 2010.</ref>

While a player for the Saints, Hargrove is alleged to have been involved in a [[New Orleans Saints bounty scandal|bounty program where coaches offered extra payments to defensive players who injured or otherwise knocked key offensive players out of the game]]. Hargrove faced an eight-game suspension in conjunction with the scandal, and was alleged to have told NFL officials that Saints coaches had instructed players to lie to league officials about the existence of the program.<ref>[http://content.usatoday.com/communities/thehuddle/post/2012/05/former-saints-lineman-anthony-hargrove-says-gregg-williams-joe-vitt-told-him-to-lie-about-bounty-program/1#.T6hZHsXhdx4 "Hargrove: Williams, Vitt Told Me to Lie About Bounty Program"] ''[[USA Today]]'', May 7, 2012.</ref>

===Philadelphia Eagles===
The [[Philadelphia Eagles]] signed Hargrove on August 3, 2011. He was released during final roster cuts on September 3.

===Seattle Seahawks===
The [[Seattle Seahawks]] signed Hargrove on September 9, 2011.

On December 18, 2011, during a game against the [[Chicago Bears]], wide receiver [[Johnny Knox]] sustained a serious back injury after attempting to recover his own fumble and awkwardly colliding with Hargrove. Knox required immediate surgery in order to stabilize an injured vertebra.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/chicago/nfl/story/_/id/7365713/chicago-bears-johnny-knox-undergo-surgery-big-hit |title=Chicago Bears' Johnny Knox to undergo surgery after big hit - ESPN Chicago |publisher=Espn.go.com |date=December 19, 2011 |access-date=September 8, 2012}}</ref> The injury forced him to retire from the NFL.

===Green Bay Packers===
The [[Green Bay Packers]] signed Hargrove on March 29, 2012.<ref>[https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/7751195/green-bay-packers-get-defensive-lineman-anthony-hargrove Packers get Anthony Hargrove]</ref>

On May 2, 2012, the NFL suspended Hargrove for the first eight games of the 2012 season after naming him as one of the ringleaders of the [[New Orleans Saints bounty scandal]].  According to the league, Hargrove signed a statement admitting his role in the scheme, and also told at least one other player that the Saints had put a bounty on [[Brett Favre]] in the 2009 NFC Championship Game.  He'd also lied to investigators when the league initially probed the Saints about the bounty scandal in 2010.<ref>[http://nfllabor.files.wordpress.com/2012/05/5-2-12-saints-players1.pdf NFL announcement of player sanctions]</ref>  Hargrove, along with the other suspended players, intends to appeal.<ref name="ESPNplayers">{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/7881761/nfl-bans-four-players-new-orleans-saints-bounty-roles|title=Jonathan Vilma banned one year|publisher=[[ESPN]]|date=May 2, 2012}}</ref> His suspension was later overturned.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/saints-player-bounty-suspensions-overturned-on-appeal-0ap1000000059459 |title=Saints player bounty suspensions overturned on appeal |work=NFL.com |access-date=September 8, 2012}}</ref>

Hargrove was released on August 24, 2012.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap1000000054088/article/anthony-hargrove-released-by-green-bay-packers?module=HP11_headline_stack |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120826013326/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap1000000054088/article/anthony-hargrove-released-by-green-bay-packers?module=HP11_headline_stack |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 26, 2012 |title=Anthony Hargrove released by Green Bay Packers |work=NFL.com |date=August 24, 2012 |access-date=September 8, 2012}}</ref>

On October 9, 2012, four weeks and three days after an internal appeals panel vacated suspensions imposed on Hargrove, Saints linebacker [[Jonathan Vilma]], Browns linebacker [[Scott Fujita]] and Saints defensive end [[Will Smith (defensive end)|Will Smith]], the league has re-issued the discipline without any changes or reductions, according to a league source. This meant that Vilma was suspended a full season, Fujita was suspended three games, Smith was suspended four games, and Hargrove was suspended eight games.<ref>{{cite web|last=Brooks|first=Matt|title=Report: NFL re-issues bounty suspensions for Saints players|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/early-lead/wp/2012/10/09/nfl-re-issues-bounty-suspensions-for-saints-players/|publisher=The Washington Times|access-date=October 9, 2012}}</ref>

On December 12, 2012, "In a sharp rebuke to his successor's handling of the NFL's bounty investigation, former commissioner Paul Tagliabue overturned the suspensions of four current and former New Orleans Saints players (including Hargrove) in a case that has preoccupied the league for almost a year."<ref>{{cite news|title=Paul Tagliabue vacates penalties|date=December 12, 2012|work=[[ESPN]]|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/8736662/paul-tagliabue-vacates-new-orleans-players-bounty-penalties}}</ref>

===Dallas Cowboys===
The [[Dallas Cowboys]] signed Anthony Hargrove on May 16, 2013.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/anthony-hargrove-joining-dallas-cowboys-in-nfl-return-0ap1000000200097|title=Anthony Hargrove joining Dallas Cowboys in NFL return|website=[[NFL.com]] }}</ref> Hargrove was released by the Cowboys on June 20.

==Personal==
When Hargrove was 6, the Brooklyn tenement where he lived with his mother and two of his four half-siblings burned down.  He lived in homeless shelters and foster care until his mother died when he was 9.  An aunt in [[Port Charlotte, Florida|Port Charlotte]] adopted him.<ref name='journey'>{{Cite news| first=Karen | last=Crouse | title=Super Bowl Is Unlikely Stopover on Player's Journey to Sobriety | date=January 31, 2010 | url =https://www.nytimes.com/2010/02/01/sports/football/01hargrove.html | work =[[The New York Times]] | access-date = February 1, 2010 }}</ref>

Hargrove has said that he began abusing drugs during his time with the Rams.  He went through a series of failed drug tests and other difficulties during his tenure with the Rams and the Bills.  After his 2008 suspension, he spent more than a year in treatment centers in South Carolina and [[North Miami Beach, Florida|North Miami Beach]].  Eight months after leaving the treatment center, he found himself back in Miami to play in the [[Super Bowl XLIV|Super Bowl]].<ref name='journey' />  In view of his comeback, Hargrove's Saints teammates voted him the winner of their 2009 [[Ed Block Courage Award]].<ref>Mike Triplett, [http://www.nola.com/saints/index.ssf/2009/12/anthony_hargrove_voted_ed_bloc.html "Anthony Hargrove voted Ed Block Courage Award winner by New Orleans Saints teammates"], ''[[Times-Picayune]]'', December 23, 2009.</ref>

In June 2011, Hargrove's older brother Terence Hargrove died after being stabbed numerous times in North Port Florida.<ref>{{Cite news | url = https://www.heraldtribune.com/story/news/2011/06/23/brother-of-nfls-hargrove-stabbed-killed-in-north-port/29026114007/ | newspaper = [[Sarasota Herald-Tribune|Herald-Tribune]] | title = Terrence Hargrove, brother of NFL's Anthony Hargrove, dies of stab wounds | date = June 23, 2011 | last = Stockton | first = Halle | access-date = September 8, 2023}}</ref>

Hargrove's daughter, Amiah, is a Freshman forward on the [[Nebraska Cornhuskers women's basketball]] team. <ref>{{cite web | url=https://huskers.com/sports/womens-basketball/roster/player/amiah-hargrove | title=Amiah Hargrove - Women's Basketball 2025-26 }}</ref>

His son, [[Tre Carroll]], was on the [[Florida Atlantic Owls men's basketball|FAU Basketball]] team that went on the run to the [[NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|Final Four]] in 2023 [[NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|NCAA March Madness]] tournament.<ref>{{Cite web |title=FAU star Tre Carroll enters the transfer portal |url=https://m.fau.edu/u/device/text-spider/news/detail?feed=university_press&id=65be77ee-f1bc-5112-a3ab-ade66d5eefc0 |access-date=2025-05-18 |website=MYFAU |language=en}}</ref>

==Current==
Hargrove has recently joined the MTV Mavericks Special Olympics team as the Speed and Agility trainer. He has also coached with [[CoachUp]].<ref>[http://www.coachup.com/coaches/anthonyh-3 www.coachup.com/coaches/anthonyh-3]</ref>

In June 2016, Hargrove became an assistant coach for the [[Christopher, Illinois|Christopher]]-[[Zeigler, Illinois|Zeigler]]-[[Royalton, Illinois|Royalton]] (CZR) team (a cooperative team that represents two high schools in [[Franklin County, Illinois]]). In June 2017 he became head coach.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Homan|first1=John|url=http://thesouthern.com/sports/sports-hargrove-brings-nfl-experience-to-czr/article_5a83ec7b-9349-507c-9e30-e4e25c80a763.html|publisher=The Southern Illinoisan|title=Anthony Hargrove named head football coach at C-Z-R|date=June 26, 2017}}</ref><ref>[http://usatodayhss.com/2017/anthony-hargrove-named-head-football-coach-at-ill-school "Ex-NFL DL Anthony Hargrove named head football coach at Ill. school"], ''[[USA Today]]'',  June 27, 2017.</ref>

In the spring of 2022, Hargrove was named the defensive line coach at Limestone University in Gaffney, SC, where he is a part of former NFL veteran Mike Furrey's staff.

==Professional career==

'''Anthony Harrison''' (born September 26, 1965) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (football position)|safety]] for the [[Green Bay Packers]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played in three games with the Packers during the [[1987 NFL season]] as a [[replacement player]] after the [[National Football League Players Association]] (NFLPA) went on strike for 24 days. Harrison played [[college football]] for the [[Georgia Institute of Technology]] before his professional career.
