'''Anthony Duane Hancock''' (born June 10, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). A first-round draft pick in the [[1982 NFL draft]], he played for five seasons with the Chiefs, retiring following the 1986 season. He played [[college football]] at the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]], leading the school in receiving in three consecutive seasons (1979–1981).

Now a teacher at Bearden Middle School in [[Knoxville, Tennessee]], Hancock is active with the Tennessee Education Association (TEA).  In 2012, he ran unsuccessfully for a seat in the [[Tennessee House of Representatives]], losing to the incumbent, [[Steve Hall (politician)|Steve Hall]].

==Early life==

Hancock was born in [[Cleveland, Ohio]].  One of nine children, his father worked for [[Ford Motor Company|Ford]].  He played [[running back]] at Cleveland's [[John Hay High School]] under Coach Sonny Harris, twice rushing for more than a thousand yards per season to win Cleveland's East League MVP honors.  During his senior year, he accumulated 1,083 yards on 153 carries, and was named all-state.  He also ran [[track and field|track]], registering a personal best of 13.6 seconds in the high hurdles.<ref name=signees>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=739&pg=57 1978 Signees] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304094256/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=739&pg=57 |date=March 4, 2016 }}, ''1978 Tennessee Volunteers Football Guide'', p. 55.</ref>

==College career==

Hancock signed to play with the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]] in 1978, part of a signing class that included future NFL players [[Mike Miller (wide receiver)|Mike Miller]], Darryal Wilson, and Terry Daniels.<ref name=signees />  Initially a running back, he switched to wide receiver a few games into the 1978 season.  His best game as a freshman came in Tennessee's loss to rival [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama]], in which he caught three passes for 52 yards.  He finished the season with seven receptions for 122 yards and a touchdown.  He also returned five kickoffs for 77 yards, and two punts for 16 yards.<ref name=79squad>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=740&pg=44 1979 Squad] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203010256/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=740&pg=44 |date=December 3, 2013 }}," ''1979 Tennessee Volunteers Football Guide'', p. 43.</ref>

Hancock entered the 1979 season one of Tennessee's key receiving threats, having caught three passes for 109 yards in the Orange-and-White Game that spring.  He finished the regular season with a team-leading 34 catches for 689 yards and four touchdowns, averaging just over 20 yards per catch.  His 85-yard touchdown reception in Tennessee's win over [[Vanderbilt Commodores football|Vanderbilt]] was, at the time, the longest in school history.<ref name=80squad />  He had a 41-yard touchdown reception earlier in the game that sparked a Tennessee rally, and finished the game with 163 receiving yards. He caught three passes for 116 yards in Tennessee's 27–22 loss to [[Purdue Boilermakers football|Purdue]] in the 1979 [[Bluebonnet Bowl]]. As a member of Tennessee's track team, he placed second in the high hurdles at the NCAA Indoor Championships.<ref name=80squad>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=741&pg=45 1980 Squad] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203005250/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=741&pg=45 |date=December 3, 2013 }}," ''1980 Tennessee Volunteers Football Guide'', p. 43.</ref>

Although Tennessee's offense struggled during the 1980 season,<ref>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=194&pg=88 Offense Remains Placid for Fourth Week] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304035434/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=194&pg=88 |date=March 4, 2016 }}," ''1981 Tennessee Volunteers Football Guide'', p. 86.</ref> Hancock nevertheless caught 33 passes for 580 yards and two touchdowns.  He also rushed 17 times (mostly on [[reverse (American football)|reverses]]) for 131 yards and a touchdown.<ref name=81squad>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=194&pg=46 1981 Squad] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304061323/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=194&pg=46 |date=March 4, 2016 }}," ''1981 Tennessee Volunteers Football Guide'', p. 44.</ref>  In the fourth quarter of Tennessee's 20–17 loss to [[Southern California Trojans football|Southern Cal]], Hancock caught a short throw from [[Steve Alatorre]] and outran the Trojan secondary for a 56-yard, game-tying touchdown.<ref name=81squad />  He finished the game with 135 receiving yards.  In Tennessee's win over [[Washington State Cougars football|Washington State]], Hancock caught a 45-yard, third-down pass in the fourth quarter to set up a touchdown and thwart a late rally by the Cougars.<ref>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=194&pg=86 Alatorre-Hancock Combo Saves Vols] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203001636/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=194&pg=86 |date=December 3, 2013 }}," ''1981 Tennessee Volunteers Football Guide'', p. 84.</ref> In Tennessee's 23–10 win over [[Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football|Georgia Tech]], Hancock caught 6 passes for 120 yards, including a 47-yard touchdown.<ref>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=194&pg=87&catid=44&s=hancock Duncan's Artistry Provides Breathing Room] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222113608/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=194&pg=87&catid=44&s=hancock |date=December 22, 2015 }}," ''1981 Tennessee Volunteers Football Guide'', p. 85.</ref>

Going into the 1981 season, Tennessee coach [[Johnny Majors]] sought to get the ball to Hancock more often, stating, "everytime he touches the ball, it seems like something good happens."<ref name=rutledge>J.D. Rutledge, "[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=223&pg=51&catid=44&s=hancock Vol Profile: Anthony Hancock] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131202234022/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=223&pg=51&catid=44&s=hancock |date=December 2, 2013 }}," ''Tennessee vs. Wichita State Football Guide'' (1981), pp. 47–48.</ref>  In spite of missing the first three games of the season with a broken foot,<ref name=rutledge /> Hancock registered 32 catches for 437 yards and 5 touchdowns, and rushed 16 times for 110 yards and a touchdown.<ref>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=742&pg=93 1981 Offensive Statistics] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131202230308/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=742&pg=93 |date=December 2, 2013 }}," ''1982 Tennessee Volunteers Football Guide'', p. 91.</ref>  In Tennessee's 10–7 win over [[Auburn Tigers football|Auburn]], Hancock picked up 21 yards on a reverse to set up the Vols' only touchdown.<ref name=rutledge />  Two weeks later against Georgia Tech, Hancock caught a 42-yard touchdown pass from Alatorre in the fourth quarter to lead the Vols to a 10–7 win.<ref name=rutledge />  He caught six passes for 75 yards in Tennessee's loss to Alabama,<ref name=rutledge /> and caught 9 passes for 60 yards in the Vols' win over [[Memphis Tigers football|Memphis State]].<ref>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=742&pg=90 Furnas' 100-yard Performance Dooms Memphis State] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203004212/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=742&pg=90 |date=December 3, 2013 }}," ''1982 Tennessee Volunteers Football Guide'', p. 88.</ref> In Tennessee's 28–21 win over Wisconsin in the [[1981 Garden State Bowl]], Hancock registered one of the best-ever postseason performances by a Vol receiver, catching 11 passes for 196 yards and a touchdown. His 11 receptions remains the most ever by a Vol receiver in a bowl game, and his 196 receiving yards is second only to [[Peerless Price]]'s 199-yard outing in the 1999 BCS National Championship Game.<ref>[http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/fball-stats/h.htm Individual Football Records] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131031142831/http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/fball-stats/h.htm |date=October 31, 2013 }}, UTSports.com, pp. 370, 386.</ref>

During his four years at Tennessee, Hancock caught 106 passes for 1,826 yards 12 touchdowns, and rushed 38 times for 262 yards and two touchdowns.<ref>[http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/fball-stats/h.htm Career Football Statistics] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131031142831/http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/fball-stats/h.htm |date=October 31, 2013 }}, UTSports.com. Retrieved: November 23, 2013.</ref>  As of the 2012 season, his total career receiving yardage was the 10th-highest in school history.<ref>[http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/fball-stats/h.htm Individual Football Records] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131031142831/http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/fball-stats/h.htm |date=October 31, 2013 }}, UTSports.com, p. 340.</ref>  Along with teammates [[Willie Gault]], [[Clyde Duncan]] and [[Lenny Taylor (American football)|Lenny Taylor]], he helped establish Tennessee's reputation as "Wide Receiver U" in the early 1980s.<ref>Mike Strange, "[http://www.knoxnews.com/news/2012/sep/30/vols-were-sugar-sweet/?print=1 Vols Were Sugar Sweet]," ''Knoxnews.com'', September 30, 2012. Retrieved: November 23, 2013.</ref>  Hancock also helped recruit fellow John Hay alumnus and future All-American receiver [[Tim McGee]] to Tennessee in 1982.<ref>Ben Byrd, "[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=199&pg=66&catid=46&s=mcgee Tim McGee: The Dean of Receivers] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131113201627/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=199&pg=66&catid=46&s=mcgee |date=November 13, 2013 }}," ''1984 Football Press Guide: UT vs. Maryland (Sun Bowl)'', p. D-8. Originally published in the ''Knoxville Journal''. Retrieved: November 23, 2013.</ref>

==Professional career==

Hancock was selected by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the first round (11th overall) of the [[1982 NFL draft]].  During his rookie year, he scored his first touchdown on a 41-yard reception in the Chiefs' 26–13 loss to [[San Francisco 49ers|San Francisco]].  His 609 kickoff return yards in 1982 included a long of 68 yards, and his 103 punt return yards included a long of 30 yards.<ref>[http://www.nfl.com/player/anthonyhancock/2515729/gamelogs?season=1982 Anthony Hancock: 1982 Game Logs], NFL.com. Retrieved: November 23, 2013.</ref>

Hancock's best NFL season, statistically, was the 1983 season, when he caught 37 passes for 584 yards and a touchdown.  He had seven catches for 87 yards in the Chiefs' 41–38 loss to [[San Diego Chargers|San Diego]], five catches for 94 yards in the Chiefs' 27–12 loss to [[Washington Redskins|Washington]], and six catches for 73 yards, including a 45-yard touchdown, in the Chiefs' second loss of the season to the Chargers, 17–14.<ref>[http://www.nfl.com/player/anthonyhancock/2515729/gamelogs?season=1983 Anthony Hancock: 1983 Game Logs], NFL.com. Retrieved: November 23, 2013.</ref>

Hancock had two strong games to open the 1984 season, catching three passes for 34 yards in the Chiefs' 37–27 win over [[Pittsburgh Steelers|Pittsburgh]], and catching three passes for 109 yards, including a 46-yard touchdown, in the Chiefs' 27–22 win over [[Cincinnati Bengals|Cincinnati]].  His production declined after the third game, however.  He finished the season with 217 yards and a touchdown on 10 catches.<ref>[http://www.nfl.com/player/anthonyhancock/2515729/gamelogs?season=1984 Anthony Hancock: 1984 Game Logs], NFL.com. Retrieved: November 23, 2013.</ref>

During the 1985 season, Hancock caught 15 passes for 286 yards and two touchdowns.  He had a 41-yard touchdown reception in the Chiefs' loss to the [[Los Angeles Raiders|Raiders]], caught three passes for 62 yards in a loss to [[Houston Oilers|Houston]], had four catches for 55 yards and a touchdown against Pittsburgh, and caught three passes for 79 yards in the Chiefs' win over [[Indianapolis Colts|Indianapolis]].<ref>[http://www.nfl.com/player/anthonyhancock/2515729/gamelogs?season=1985 Anthony Hancock: 1985 Game Logs], NFL.com. Retrieved: November 23, 2013.</ref>  He was released after the 1986 season.<ref name=huntoon>Paige Huntoon, "[https://web.archive.org/web/20131203030827/http://www.metropulse.com/news/2012/oct/17/volunteer-candidate-profile-anthony-hancock-runnin/ The Volunteer: Candidate Profile of Anthony Hancock, Running for the 18th District Seat in the State Legislature]," ''Metro Pulse'', October 17, 2012. Accessed at the Internet Archive, October 2, 2015.</ref>

==Post-playing career==

Hancock returned to Knoxville in 1986, and was hired by the [[Boy Scouts of America]] to run its inner city scouting program.  During his tenure, he recruited over 500 new scouts, 12 of whom became [[Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)|Eagle Scout]]s.<ref name=huntoon />  He also worked with UT's Institute of Public Service, a role in which he advised [[Tennessee Department of Transportation|TDOT]]-certified small businesses on financial planning and bidding.<ref name=huntoon />  In the early 2000s, he began working for [[Knox County Schools]], initially as a substitute teacher, before obtaining his special education certificate from UT.  He currently works as a special education teacher at Bearden Middle School.<ref name=huntoon />  He has been active with the state's teachers' union, the Tennessee Education Association, serving on the TEA's board of directors,<ref>[http://teateachers.org/board-directors Board of Directors], Tennessee Education Association official website.  Retrieved: November 23, 2013.</ref> as well as chair of the group's resolution committee.<ref name=huntoon />

In 2012, Hancock, a [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]], ran against the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Steve Hall (politician)|Steve Hall]] for the 18th District's seat in the [[Tennessee House of Representatives]].<ref name=huntoon /> He campaigned on a platform of fostering an environment for small business innovation and expanding technology in schools, and pledged to keep taxes low.<ref name=blackerby>Mike Blackerby, "[http://www.knoxnews.com/news/2012/nov/06/hall-re-elected-to-2nd-term/ Steve Hall Re-elected to 2nd Term]," ''Knoxville News Sentinel'', November 6, 2012. Retrieved: November 23, 2013.</ref>  In October 2012, he appeared at a campaign stop with his former coach, Johnny Majors.<ref>"[http://www.wate.com/story/19778837/majors-held-rally-for-former-player-hancock?clienttype=printable Johnny Majors Holds Political Rally for Former Player Anthony Hancock] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203165438/http://www.wate.com/story/19778837/majors-held-rally-for-former-player-hancock?clienttype=printable |date=December 3, 2013 }}," WATE.com, October 9, 2012. Retrieved: November 23, 2013</ref>  On election day, he captured just 37.5% of the vote in the heavily Republican district.<ref name=blackerby />

SWAC Coach of the Year (2006) | coaching_records = }} '''Anthony Andrew Jones''' (born May 16, 1960) is an American [[American football|football]] coach and former player. He was most recently the head football coach at [[Elizabeth City State University]], a position he has held from 2018 to 2021. He served as head coach at [[Morehouse College]] from 1999 to 2001, and [[Alabama Agricultural and Mechanical University]] from 2002 to 2013,. Jones played eight seasons as a [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Washington Redskins]] and [[San Diego Chargers]] during the 1980s. He was a member of the Redskins' 1987 [[Super Bowl XXII|Super Bowl]] championship team. ==Playing career== Jones initially attended the [[University of Maryland Eastern Shore]] but then transferred to [[Wichita State University]] where he played for head coach [[Willie Jeffries]]. He earned several honors as a [[tight end]], including the Ben Hustle Award (1981) and All-[[Missouri Valley Conference]] recognition (1983). Following his senior season with the Shockers, Jones was selected in the eleventh round of the [[1984 NFL draft]] by the [[Washington Redskins]].{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/J/JoneAn21.htm |title=Anthony Jones NFL Football Statistics |work=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |access-date=December 3, 2013}} He went on to play eight seasons for the team, helping to win a [[Super Bowl XXII|Super Bowl]] championship in 1987. The Redskins traded him to the [[San Diego Chargers]] during the 1988 season, but Jones was forced to retire after suffering a knee injury before the next season. ==Coaching career== ===Morehouse=== Jones's first head coaching job was at Morehouse College in Atlanta, Georgia, where he spent four years. After serving as the offensive coordinator and assistant head coach in his first year with the Maroon Tigers, he was promoted to head coach in 1999. After going 2–8 in his first season, Jones led the Tigers to the first back-to-back eight-win seasons in school history. He was named SIAC Coach of the year both times. The 2000 campaign (8-3) qualified him and the Tigers as the second-most improved team in NCAA Division II. Following his second consecutive eight-win season (8-2), Jones was one of three finalists for the 2001 Eddie Robinson Coach of the year Award along with Doug Williams (Grambling State) and Rick Comegy (Tuskegee). ===Alabama A&M=== In 2006, Jones led the Bulldogs to their first SWAC title and tied the school record with nine victories. The Bulldogs posted back-to-back nine-win seasons in 2005 and 2006. The 2006 SWAC Coach of the year has led A&M to four SWAC title games in nine seasons and enters the 2011 campaign with an 82–54 career record. With his 79–47 record while at Alabama A&M, Jones' 79 wins at A&M rank second all-time behind legendary A&M coach Louis Crews, who won 93 games at A&M. In 2005, Jones led the Bulldogs to their second SWAC East Championship under his reign, and a 9–3 record. The nine wins also earned Jones a milestone victory in the regular season finale, a 31–16 win at Prairie View served as the 50th win in Jones' career. After the Bulldogs posted tremendous 8-4 records in each of his first two seasons in 2002 and 2003, the team from the Rocket City capped off another outstanding season in 2004 with a 7–4 mark. With a 21–7 victory in the Magic City Classic Jones is 7–2 in his nine seasons against in-state rival Alabama State. The 2005, 2006, 2007 and 2009 teams also captured the John Merritt Classic title, defeating Tennessee State in the season-opener. Alabama A&M remains the only visiting team to have beaten Tennessee State in the John Merritt Classic's history. Three times, Jones has led A&M to six-game winning streaks in his tenure. After two early losses in 2002, Jones' Bulldogs won six straight and eight of nine to finish the regular season. The Bulldogs captured the SWAC East (6-1). This led to A&M's second berth in the SWAC championship in three years. In 2005, after a disappointing Homecoming loss to Texas Southern, the Bulldogs regrouped and won six straight games to finish the regular season en route to another SWAC East title and a berth in the SWAC Championship game. The 2009 season saw three two game win streaks and victories over Jackson State (13-5) and Mississippi Valley (17-12) in the final two contest of the season to earn Jones his fourth SWAC East championship and title game appearance. Jones has led A&M to five division championships in his 11 years as head coach - the most successful run in the history of the SWAC championship game. On December 1, 2013, it was announced that Jones would not return as Alabama A&M head coach. Jones served as Alabama A&M football coach for 12 seasons. ===Elizabeth City State=== On April 2, 2018, Jones was named as the head football coach for the Elizabeth City State University Vikings. ECSU competes in the Central Intercollegiate Athletic Association (CIAA). ==Family== Jones' son Julian was a top football recruit out of [[Hazel Green High School]] in Alabama. The 16-year-old junior committed suicide on October 6, 2014. '''Anthony Charles Dickerson''' (June 9, 1957 – March 21, 2019) was an American professional [[Gridiron football|football]] [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] and [[Buffalo Bills]]. He played [[college football]] at [[Southern Methodist University]].

==Early life==
Dickerson's family moved to Pearland in 1957, but it was not until after integration that he attended Pearland schools. Before the third grade he attended Ralph A Bunch in [[Manvel, Texas]]. At [[Pearland High School|Pearland (TX)]], he was a three-year starter at [[running back]] and also played [[linebacker]]. He received [[All-American]] honors as a senior.

He began his college career at [[Trinity Valley Community College|Henderson County Junior College]], where he was a Junior College [[All-American]] and an All-conference [[linebacker]] in 1976.

In 1977, Dickerson transferred to [[Southern Methodist University]] where he was named co-captain and a starter at [[linebacker]], finishing with 136 tackles (62 solo), one safety, one caused fumble, and one blocked kick. He also had a game against [[Ohio State University]] where he recorded 32 tackles. In 1978, he was let go by [[head coach]] [[Ron Meyer]]. Meyer was quoted as saying "I haven't been around that long, but Dickerson was the greatest linebacker I have ever coached".
 
On October 1, 2011, he was inducted into the [[Trinity Valley Community College]] Cardinal Hall of Fame.

==Professional career==

===Toronto Argonauts===
In [[1978 CFL season|1978]], he signed with the [[Toronto Argonauts]] of the [[Canadian Football League]]. He was waived on October 3.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1946&dat=19781004&id=q700AAAAIBAJ&sjid=8qEFAAAAIBAJ&pg=3512,969111 | title=Sports Shorts | accessdate=January 6, 2018}}</ref>

===Calgary Stampeders===
In [[1978 CFL season|1978]], he signed with the [[Calgary Stampeders]] of the [[Canadian Football League]] and played in 10 games before being released.

===Dallas Cowboys===
After being cut by the [[Calgary Stampeders]], he moved to Los Angeles and got a job as a maintenance department stock clerk at the [[Burbank Airport]]. In 1979, he returned to Texas and was taking business courses at the [[University of Houston]], when the [[Dallas Cowboys]] signed him as an [[undrafted free agent]] in [[1980 NFL season|1980]]. He made the team because he was one of the fastest [[linebacker]]s in the [[NFL]].

As a rookie, he contributed on [[special teams]] and in the [[nickel defense]], replacing [[weakside linebacker]] [[D. D. Lewis (linebacker, born 1945)|D. D. Lewis]] on passing downs. He posted 41 tackles, 2 interceptions, 6 passes defensed, 3 forced fumbles (tied for the team lead), one sack and one fumble recovery. He was named the Cowboys special teams player of the year. He had 2 interceptions against the [[San Francisco 49ers]] and caused 2 fumbles on [[special teams]] against the [[Seattle Seahawks]], that led to 2 [[touchdown]]s. In the playoffs, he recovered a fumble against the [[Atlanta Falcons]] that set up the Cowboys' first [[touchdown]] and he intercepted a pass against the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] in the NFC title game.

In [[1981 NFL season|1981]], he was named [[special teams]] captain and repeated as the Cowboys [[special teams]] player of the year. He also played on the [[nickel defense]], registering 39 tackles, 4 sacks and 2 fumble recoveries. His first half fumble recovery was a key play in the team's division title clinching 21–10 win over the [[Philadelphia Eagles]].

In [[1982 NFL season|1982]], he remained a regular player on passing downs because of his ability to cover [[running back]]s, tallying 33 tackles, 2.5 sacks and one interception.

In [[1983 NFL season|1983]], he was named the starter at [[weakside linebacker]] after [[Guy Brown]] retired. He finished with 114 tackles (second on the team), 81 solo tackles (led the team), 6 passes defensed, 2 forced fumbles, 3 fumble recoveries, one interception and 10.5 sacks (second on the team), the most ever by a [[linebacker]] in franchise history (it was broken by [[DeMarcus Ware]] in [[2006 NFL season|2006]]). Against the [[Oakland Raiders]], he tallied 11 tackles, 2 sacks, 2 forced fumbles and one fumble recovery. Against the [[New Orleans Saints]], he sacked [[Ken Stabler]] for a safety with 1:58 minutes remaining to give Dallas a 21–20 win. His pressure on [[Scott Brunner]] caused [[Dextor Clinkscale]]'s interception for the decisive [[touchdown]] in a 28–13 win over the [[New York Giants]].

Dickerson entered the [[1984 NFL season|1984 season]] as a rising star, but the team decided to alternate him with first round draft choice [[Billy Cannon Jr.]] He also was limited in the preseason with a shoulder injury. His production would drop to 72 tackles, 2 sacks, one interception and one fumble recovery. Against the [[Green Bay Packers]], he intercepted a pass in the last two minutes to set up a Cowboys [[touchdown]] in a 20–6 win. Against the [[Indianapolis Colts]], he recovered a fumble on the eight-yard line to prevent a [[touchdown]] in a 22–3 win.

On September 2, [[1985 NFL season|1985]], he was traded to the [[Buffalo Bills]] in exchange for a seventh-round draft selection in the [[1986 NFL draft]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1899&dat=19850903&id=AolGAAAAIBAJ&sjid=kPIMAAAAIBAJ&pg=1370,99174 | title=Not easy to trade a veteran | accessdate=January 6, 2018}}</ref>

===Buffalo Bills===
In [[1985 NFL season|1985]], he played mainly on [[special teams]] and did not start any games. He was released on August 11, [[1986 NFL season|1986]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1291&dat=19860812&id=Kf1TAAAAIBAJ&sjid=1YwDAAAAIBAJ&pg=3379,2731605 | title=Transactions | accessdate=January 6, 2018}}</ref>

===Miami Dolphins===
On August 14, [[1986 NFL season|1985]], he signed as a [[free agent]] with the [[Miami Dolphins]], who were having health problems with their [[outside linebacker]]s.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/157677188/| title=Browns-Dolphins Rematch Tonight | accessdate=January 6, 2018}}</ref> He was cut on August 19.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1986-08-20/sports/8602190416_1_coach-shula-dan-sekanovich-competitive-camp | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141104011125/http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1986-08-20/sports/8602190416_1_coach-shula-dan-sekanovich-competitive-camp | url-status=dead | archive-date=November 4, 2014 | title=Cuts Ease Out Barnett, Shake Wickersham | accessdate=January 6, 2018}}</ref>

'''Anthony Rishard''' "'''Boobie'''" '''Dixon''' (born September 24, 1987)<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mstateathletics.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=90891&SPID=10997&DB_OEM_ID=16800&ATCLID=944517&Q_SEASON=2009 |title=Anthony Dixon Bio |publisher=SECsports.com |access-date=August 8, 2009}}</ref><ref name="Boobie">{{cite web| url = http://www.buffalonews.com/sports/bills-nfl/bills-hope-dixon-boosts-special-teams-20140316| url-status = dead| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140318004134/http://www.buffalonews.com/sports/bills-nfl/bills-hope-dixon-boosts-special-teams-20140316| archive-date = 2014-03-18| title = Bills hope Dixon boosts special teams - Sports - The Buffalo News}}</ref> is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in the sixth round of the [[2010 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Mississippi State Bulldogs football|Mississippi State Bulldogs]], with whom he holds multiple school [[Mississippi State Bulldogs football statistical leaders#Rushing|rushing records]].

==Early life==
As a senior at [[Hinds County School District|Terry High School]] in 2005, he racked up 304 carries for 2,683 yards (8.8 average) and 31 touchdowns in leading Terry to an 11–2 mark. He was named the [[Jackson, Mississippi metropolitan area|Jackson metro-area]] player of the year by ''[[The Clarion-Ledger]]''. He was also a first-team All-State honoree by the paper, and was named to its (preseason) "Dandy Dozen" team (of the state's 12 best high school players) and its (postseason) "10 Most Wanted" list (of the state's top 10 [[college football]] prospects).

Considered a four-star recruit by ''[[Rivals.com]]'', Dixon was listed as the No. 22 running back prospect in the nation in 2006.<ref>{{Citation |url=https://footballrecruiting.rivals.com/viewrank.asp?ra_key=1146 |title=Running backs 2006 |work=Rivals.com |date=January 30, 2006 |access-date=April 19, 2014 |archive-date=August 24, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070824073415/http://footballrecruiting.rivals.com/viewrank.asp?ra_key=1146 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Scout.com ranked Dixon a four star prospect and the 30th best running back in the country.<ref>{{Citation | url=http://recruiting.scout.com/a.z?s=73&p=8&c=1&nid=1897890 |title = Anthony Dixon Scout.com profile page |work=Scout.com | date=January 1, 2006 }}</ref>

He chose Mississippi State over [[University of Alabama]], [[Louisiana State University]], and [[University of Southern Mississippi|Southern Miss]].

==College career==
In his true freshman season at [[Mississippi State University]], Dixon played in all 12 games, starting five times, and set MSU true freshman records for rushing attempts, yards gained rushing, and touchdowns rushing. His nine touchdowns on the ground were the most by a [[Mississippi State Bulldogs football|Bulldog]] since [[Dicenzo Miller]]'s ten TDs in 2000. He earned his nickname "Boobie" from his college teammates, who compared him to [[Boobie Miles]], the character in ''[[Friday Night Lights: A Town, a Team, and a Dream|Friday Night Lights]]''.<ref name="Boobie"/>

As a sophomore, Dixon played all 13 games and started twelve. He became just the seventh halfback (ninth occurrence) in school history and the first Bulldog sophomore ever to surpass 1,000 yards rushing in a single season and his attempts set a Mississippi State single season record. He scored MSU's game-winning touchdown in the [[2007 Liberty Bowl]] game.

During his junior season, Dixon started all 12 games he played in, and rushed for 869 yards, compiling a career-best 4.4 yards per carry.

With 1,391 rushing yards in his senior season, Dixon not only set the Mississippi State single-season rushing record (surpassing [[J. J. Johnson (running back)|J. J. Johnson]]'s 1998 record of 1,383 yards), he also became the seventh player in [[Southeastern Conference]] history to lead his team in rushing four times. He joined [[Eddie Price]] ([[Tulane Green Wave football|Tulane]], 1946–1949), [[Sonny Collins]] ([[Kentucky Wildcats football|Kentucky]], 1972–1975), [[Dalton Hilliard]] ([[LSU Tigers football|LSU]], 1982–1985), [[Carl Woods]] ([[Vanderbilt Commodores football|Vanderbilt]], 1983–1986), [[Errict Rhett]] ([[Florida Gators football|Florida]], 1990–1993), and [[Kevin Faulk]] (LSU, 1995–1998) on that list. Dixon accumulated 3,994 career rushing yards during his collegiate career.<ref>{{Citation |url=http://blog.al.com/press-register-sports/2009/11/sec_football_by_the_numbers_ex.html |title=Mississippi State's Anthony Dixon joining short list of SEC ballcarriers |last=Inabinett |first=Mark |date=November 28, 2009 |newspaper=Mobile Press-Register }}</ref>

==Professional career==

===2010 NFL draft===
Dixon was considered one of the best "power backs" available in the [[2010 NFL draft]], alongside [[Toby Gerhart]] and [[Charles Scott (American football)|Charles Scott]].<ref>{{Citation |url=http://www.cbssports.com/nfl/draft/prospectrankings/TSX/2010_RB |title=NFL Draft - 2010 RB Draft Prospects |work=CBSSports.com |access-date=November 25, 2009 }}</ref> Projected as a third- to fourth-round pick, Dixon was thought to possibly be the Bulldogs' highest draftee since [[Jerious Norwood]] was selected by the [[Atlanta Falcons]] in the third round (79th overall) of the [[2006 NFL draft]].<ref name="Miller Dispatch">{{Citation |url=http://www.cdispatch.com/sports/article.asp?aid=4993 |title=Chaney, Dixon hope to impress at NFL Combine |first=David |last=Miller |date=February 24, 2010 |newspaper=The Dispatch }}.</ref> However, he was selected as the 173rd overall pick in the sixth round by the [[San Francisco 49ers]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2010 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2010/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-13 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

===San Francisco 49ers===
[[File:Anthony Dixon.JPG|thumb|Dixon with the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in 2012]]
With the announcement of the sudden retirement of [[Glen Coffee]] on August 13, former head coach [[Mike Singletary]] stated that Dixon and veteran [[Michael Robinson (running back)|Michael Robinson]] would compete for the number 2 running back spot behind Pro Bowler [[Frank Gore]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blog.49ers.com/2010/08/13/coffee-tells-49ers-he-intends-to-retire/ |title=Coffee Tells 49ers He Intends to Retire |author=Price, Taylor |date=August 13, 2010 |publisher=San Francisco 49ers |access-date=August 14, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100816122157/http://blog.49ers.com/2010/08/13/coffee-tells-49ers-he-intends-to-retire/ |archive-date=August 16, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In the preseason, Dixon posted 74 rushes for 300 yards, averaging 75 yards per game and 4 touchdowns, leading the entire NFL in each of those categories. On September 20, 2010, Dixon rushed for his first career NFL touchdown against the [[New Orleans Saints]] on ''[[Monday Night Football]]''. Despite playing well in the preseason, Dixon had only ten rushing attempts until week 12. After Gore suffered a fractured hip during a ''Monday Night Football'' game against the [[Arizona Cardinals]] on November 29, Dixon had 14 carries for 54 yards and a touchdown as a backup to [[Brian Westbrook]], who took over for Gore. Dixon  played in all 72 games of his NFL career, primarily on [[special teams]]. At the end of the 2012 season, Dixon and the 49ers appeared in [[Super Bowl XLVII]]. He contributed on special teams, but the 49ers fell to the [[Baltimore Ravens]] by a score of 34–31.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201302030sfo.htm |title=Super Bowl XLVII - San Francisco 49ers vs. Baltimore Ravens - February 3rd, 2013 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |access-date=December 2, 2017}}</ref> His only start as a member of the 49ers came in the 2013 NFC Championship game as a [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]], scoring a touchdown that gave San Francisco a 10–0 lead. Coincidentally, that was his last game as a member of the 49ers.  He finished his 49er career with 458 regular-season rushing yards and eight touchdowns.<ref name="Bills add Anthony Dixon">[http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2014/03/15/bills-add-anthony-dixon/ Bills add Anthony Dixon]</ref><ref>[http://www.ninersnation.com/2014/3/14/5510522/nfl-free-agency-news-anthony-dixon-signing-bills NFL free agency news: Anthony Dixon signing with Buffalo Bills]</ref>

===Buffalo Bills===
On March 15, 2014, Dixon signed a three-year, $3.5 million contract with the [[Buffalo Bills]].<ref name="Bills add Anthony Dixon"/> Dixon went on to have the most productive year of his career, with career highs in rushing attempts (105), rushing yards (432), average yards per rush (4.1), as well as passes caught and receiving yardage (eight catches for 49 yards). Dixon also scored two rushing touchdowns, the same number he had scored each year since entering the NFL.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anthony Dixon 2014 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/D/DixoAn00/gamelog/2014/ |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

In 2015, Dixon's production dropped off significantly. He had only one rushing touchdown, and recorded both 44 yards rushing and 44 yards receiving.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anthony Dixon 2015 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/D/DixoAn00/gamelog/2015/ |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> On March 1, 2016, Dixon was released by the Bills.<ref name="x612">{{cite web | last=Rapp | first=Timothy | title=Anthony Dixon Released by Bills: Latest Details, Comments and Reaction | website=Bleacher Report | date=2016-03-01 | url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2620998-anthony-dixon-released-by-bills-latest-details-comments-and-reaction | access-date=2024-12-27}}</ref>

===The Spring League===
After spending the 2016 season out of football, Dixon played in front of NFL and [[Canadian Football League]] scouts as part of the inaugural season for a new instructional and developmental football program, [[The Spring League]], taking part in both the April training camp and games held at [[The Greenbrier]] in [[West Virginia]], as well as the 2017 Summer Showcase game held in [[Napa, California]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Former Bills RB Fred Jackson to participate in Spring League|url=http://www.wkbw.com/sports/bills/former-bills-rb-fred-jackson-to-participate-in-spring-league|first=Nick|last=Filipowski|work=WKBW-TV|date=June 19, 2017|access-date=June 20, 2017}}</ref> As one of The Spring League's "marquee players"<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.thespringleague.com/about/|title = Home}}</ref> Dixon was one of the more vocal players in the league, and predicted he would amass 100 yards and 2 touchdowns during the California Showcase game. Playing as part of team California, Dixon's teammate included fellow running back [[Glen Coffee]],<ref name="e679">{{cite web | last=Fucillo | first=David | title=Glen Coffee to take part in Spring League Showcase game in Napa on July 15 | website=Niners Nation | date=2017-07-11 | url=https://www.ninersnation.com/2017/7/11/15951904/glen-coffee-comeback-spring-league-showcase-game-july-15-location-napa | access-date=2024-11-29}}</ref> the player Dixon replaced as a member of the 49ers. Playing predominately as a fullback, Dixon's first carry was a 49-yard touchdown run. Late in the game, Dixon caught a 4-yard touchdown pass from [[David Ash (American football)|David Ash]].<ref name="v282">{{cite web | last=D'Adamo | first=Vince | title=Spring League game at Napa Memorial Stadium keeps football dreams alive | website=The Napa Valley Register | date=2024-10-18 | url=https://napavalleyregister.com/sports/college-and-pro/spring-league-game-at-napa-memorial-stadium-keeps-football-dreams/article_cbc5e5e0-1c16-5384-8d3d-802552e23f9f.html | access-date=2024-11-29}}</ref> Both plays occurred on 4th down, and were the first and last scores of the game, respectively. Dixon's totals were 7 carries for 55 yards, 5 catches for 23 yards, and the two touchdowns. With 78 total yards on 12 touches, Dixon was short of his statistical pregame prediction, but nonetheless he was listed as one of the Stand Out Players of the game during the Summer Showcase broadcast.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.flofootball.com/video/1227387-spring-league-showcase-full-replay|title=Spring League Showcase Full Game Replay}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Dixon is a [[Christianity|Christian]]. Dixon describes himself on his Twitter account as a "[[God in Christianity|God]] Fearing Man" and frequently tweets about his faith.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://twitter.com/Boobie24Dixon| title=Anthony Dixon}}</ref>

Anthony also has three younger brothers Antwon, Rashun, and Deshun (from oldest to youngest).  Antwon and Rashun  both committed to play football at Mississippi State, although neither played at MSU.  Antwon instead went to  [[Hinds Community College]] before transferring to [[Midwestern State Mustangs|Midwestern State University]].  Rashun was selected in the 10th round (304th overall) in the [[2008 Major League Baseball draft]] by the [[Oakland As]] and chose to play professional baseball.  Deshun was also drafted by in the [[MLB draft]], taken in the 10th round by the Tampa Bay Rays in the [[2010 Major League Baseball draft]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://msumustangs.com/roster.aspx?rp_id=1262|title=MSU Mustangs Bio for Antwon Dixon|access-date=October 31, 2014}}</ref>

'''Anthony Collins''' (born November 2, 1985) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Kansas Jayhawks football|Kansas Jayhawks]] and was a member of their [[2008 Orange Bowl]] championship team. Collins was selected by the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] in the fourth round of the [[2008 NFL draft]]. He also played for the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]].

==Early life==
Collins played [[high school football]] at [[Central High School (Beaumont, Texas)|Central High School]] in [[Beaumont, Texas]].

==College career==
Collins committed to the [[University of Kansas]] out of high school. He redshirted his freshman year. During the [[Kansas Jayhawks football|Jayhawks]] [[2007 Kansas Jayhawks football team|2007 season]], his redshirt junior year, he helped lead the Jayhawks to their first and only [[Bowl Championship Series|BCS]] Bowl victory in the [[2008 Orange Bowl]]. Collins and teammate [[Aqib Talib]] were both named 1st team [[2007 College Football All-America Team|AP All-Americans]] that season.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tebow, McFadden, Smith on AP All-America first team|url=http://www.espn.com/ncf/news/story?id=3150439|website=ESPN.com| date=11 December 2007 }}</ref>

Collins was added to the Ring of Honor during the Jayhawks [[2017 Kansas Jayhawks football team|2017 season]] along with his teammate from the 2007 Orange Bowl Championship season, Aqib Talib.<ref>{{cite web|title=Kansas Athletics to honor 2007 Orange Bowl team, Aqib Talib, Anthony Collins and Mark Mangino at September 2 home-opener|url=http://kuathletics.com/news/2017/8/15/football-kansas-athletics-to-honor-2007-orange-bowl-team-aqib-talib-anthony-collins-and-mark-mangino-at-september-2-home-opener.aspx|website=KUAthletics.com|date=15 August 2017 }}</ref>

==Professional career==

===Cincinnati Bengals===
Collins played for the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] from 2008 to 2013, after being drafted in the fourth round with the 112th pick of the [[2008 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2008 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2008/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Most of his career was spent as a rotational player at [[left guard]] and [[left tackle]]. During his 2013 campaign, he had his strongest year, consistently performing well on the Bengals' offensive line as a left tackle.

===Tampa Bay Buccaneers===
On March 13, 2014, Collins signed a contract with the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.buccaneers.com/news/article-smith/Busy-Bucs-Add-Collins-to-Boost-O-Line/9915208c-e2fd-4946-abf8-31324aa27216 |title=Busy Bucs Add Collins to Boost O-Line |access-date=2014-03-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140314030549/http://www.buccaneers.com/news/article-smith/Busy-Bucs-Add-Collins-to-Boost-O-Line/9915208c-e2fd-4946-abf8-31324aa27216 |archive-date=2014-03-14 |url-status=dead }}</ref> However, health concerns, multiple penalties and inconsistent play led to Collins being benched in favor of veteran right tackle [[Demar Dotson]]. He was considered more of a liability with his penalties and pedestrian play in the pass rush situations.

On March 2, 2015 it was announced that Tampa would try to trade Collins or release him, confirming that he would not be brought back for the 2015 season. On March 10, 2015, the team released Collins after failing to trade him before the official start of free agency.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.buccaneers.com/news/article-smith/Bucs-Release-Collins-Among-Roster-Moves/f491d9fb-1d71-4f83-8131-36ae17c14f68|title=Bucs Release Collins Among Roster Moves|first=Scott|last=Smith|date=March 10, 2015|accessdate=March 11, 2015|work=Buccaneers.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150311150010/http://www.buccaneers.com/news/article-smith/Bucs-Release-Collins-Among-Roster-Moves/f491d9fb-1d71-4f83-8131-36ae17c14f68|archive-date=March 11, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>

'''Anthony Nathaniel Davis''' (born October 11, 1989) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] for the [[San Francisco 49ers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Rutgers Scarlet Knights football|Rutgers Scarlet Knights]] and was selected by the 49ers in the first round of the [[2010 NFL draft]].

==Early life==
Davis attended [[Piscataway Township High School]] in [[New Jersey]], where he played for the Piscataway Chiefs [[high school football]] team. He was a three-year starter and recorded more than 70 [[pancake blocks]] for his career. In his sophomore season, Davis was a teammate to fellow NFL players [[Kyle Wilson (cornerback)|Kyle Wilson]], and [[Malcolm Jenkins]] and helped the team to an undefeated season, and its third consecutive state title.  Davis played in the [[U.S. Army All-American Bowl]] and was earned First-team All-American honors by ''[[USA Today]]''.

Considered a four-star recruit by [[Rivals.com]], Davis was listed as the No. 1 offensive tackle  prospect in the nation.<ref>{{Citation |date=January 24, 2007 |title=Rivals.com offensive guards 2007 |url=https://footballrecruiting.rivals.com/viewrank.asp?ra_key=1481&Year=2007 }}</ref> He was also listed as the top prospect coming out of high school in the nation.<ref name=Rivals.com>{{cite web|title=Rivals.Com Ranking|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/highschool/football/recruiting/rankings/rank-1475|work=High School Rankings|publisher=Rivals.Com|access-date=March 23, 2011}}</ref>  He was also regarded as the top prospect from New Jersey and received over 50 scholarship offers, he chose Rutgers over [[Ohio State University|Ohio State]], becoming the first No. 1 prospect from New Jersey to sign with head coach [[Greg Schiano]] at Rutgers, and the highest rated since [[Nate Robinson (American football)|Nate Robinson]] in 2003.

==College career==
In his freshman year at Rutgers, Davis played in all 13 games on the year. He was named starting right guard for the sixth game of the season and started the final eight games of the [[2007 NCAA Division I FBS football season|2007 season]]. He earned First-team Freshman All-American honors by the ''[[Football Writers Association of America]]'',<ref>{{Citation |publisher=FWAA |date=January 7, 2008 |title=AON Insurance/FWAA Freshman All-America Team 2007 |url=http://www.sportswriters.net/fwaa/news/2007/allamerica080107.html }}</ref> ''[[The Sporting News]]'' and ''Rivals.com'', and Second-team All-American laurels from ''[[Scout.com]]''.

Davis was moved to left tackle before the [[2008 NCAA Division I FBS football season|2008 season]], and started 12 games at that position. He was named to the Second-team All-Big East by the league's head coaches and a First-team All-Big East honoree by the media.

In 2009, Davis was First-team All-Big East and Second-team All-America.

After the [[2009 St. Petersburg Bowl]], Davis said on the field that he scheduled a news conference for December 22, to announce his NFL plans.<ref name="Schad ESPN">{{Citation |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/draft10/news/story?id=4758405 |work=ESPN.com |last=Schad |first=Joe |title=Sources: Rutgers offensive lineman Anthony Davis to enter NFL Draft |date=December 20, 2009 }}</ref> At that news conference, he declared his intentions to enter the [[2010 NFL draft]], and said he would hire an agent.<ref>{{Citation |url=http://www.nj.com/rutgersfootball/index.ssf/2009/12/rutgers_lt_anthony_davis.html |title=Rutgers left tackle Anthony Davis announces he will enter NFL Draft |first=Tom |last=Luicci |newspaper=The Star-Ledger |date=December 22, 2009 }}</ref>

Davis was drafted in the first round with the 11th overall pick by the [[San Francisco 49ers]] after the 49ers traded up from the 13th overall pick with the [[Denver Broncos]] in order to select Davis.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2010 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2010/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-13 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> On July 30, 2010, Davis signed a five-year contract worth $37.5 million, with $15.95 million guaranteed.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://content.usatoday.com/communities/thehuddle/post/2010/07/49ers-come-to-terms-with-first-round-pick-anthony-davis/1 | work=USA Today | title=49ers come to terms with first-round pick Anthony Davis | date=July 30, 2010}}</ref>

At the end of the 2012 season, Davis and the 49ers appeared in [[Super Bowl XLVII]]. He started in the game, but the 49ers fell to the [[Baltimore Ravens]] by a score of 34–31.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201302030sfo.htm |title=Super Bowl XLVII - San Francisco 49ers vs. Baltimore Ravens - February 3rd, 2013 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=December 2, 2017}}</ref>

On June 5, 2015, Davis announced he would not be playing during the 2015 season, stating he wanted time to "let his brain and body heal".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ballerstatus.com/2015/06/06/49ers-tackle-anthony-davis-announces-retirement/ |title=49ers' Tackle Anthony Davis Announces Retirement|publisher=BallerStatus.com |date=June 6, 2015}}</ref> He vowed a return after the break, however, claiming he wanted to return as the best right tackle in the league.<ref>{{cite web|title=Former 49ers first-round pick Anthony Davis talks comeback|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/2015/08/11/former-49ers-first-round-pick-anthony-davis-talks-comeback/31483141/|publisher=USA Today|access-date=August 12, 2015}}</ref> On July 25, 2016, Davis filed reinstatement paperwork aiming to return to the team by the start of training camp.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Sessler|first1=Marc|title=Retired RT Anthony Davis applies for reinstatement|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/retired-rt-anthony-davis-applies-for-reinstatement-0ap3000000676557|website=NFL.com|access-date=July 26, 2016}}</ref> On July 30, Davis was officially reinstated by the league and re-joined the 49ers in time for their [[training camp]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Fucillo|first1=David|title=Anthony Davis reinstated by NFL, reporting to 49ers training camp today|url=http://www.ninersnation.com/2016/7/30/12331590/anthony-davis-reporting-to-49ers-training-camp-today|website=NinersNation.com|access-date=July 30, 2016}}</ref> On September 26, 2016, Davis announced his decision to retire again from the league,<ref>{{cite web|last1=Rosenthal|first1=Gregg|title=Niners OT Anthony Davis retires from football, again|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/niners-ot-anthony-davis-retires-again-from-football-0ap3000000710520|website=NFL.com|access-date=September 27, 2016}}</ref> and was subsequently placed on the reserve/left squad list.

On May 3, 2019, he applied for reinstatement from retirement.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2019/05/03/anthony-davis-seeks-reinstatement/|title=Anthony Davis seeks reinstatement|last=Florio|first=Mike|date=2019-05-03|website=ProFootballTalk|language=en|access-date=2019-05-04}}</ref> On May 28, 2019, he was released from the 49ers' reserve/left squad list.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sacbee.com/sports/nfl/san-francisco-49ers/article230914053.html|title=In and out with the old: 49ers make roster moves surrounding familiar names|access-date=May 29, 2019|via=Sacramento Bee}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Madson |first=Kyle |date=May 28, 2019 |title=49ers cut ties with former 1st-round pick Anthony Davis |url=https://ninerswire.usatoday.com/2019/05/28/report-49ers-cut-ties-with-former-1st-round-pick-anthony-davis/ |access-date=May 29, 2019 |website=Niners Wire|publisher=USA Today}}</ref>

'''Oscar Anthony Henton''' (born July 27,  1963) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who played two seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]].

==Early life==
Henton was born in [[Bessemer, Alabama]] where he later attended [[Jess Lanier High School]].<ref name="DBFbio">{{cite web|url=http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=HENTOANT01 |title=Anthony Henton bio |publisher=databaseFootball |accessdate=March 15, 2010 |url-status=usurped |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110610081546/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=HENTOANT01 |archivedate=June 10, 2011 }}</ref>

He  matriculated at [[Troy State University]].<ref   name="DBFbio"/>

==College career==
Henton attended Troy State University, Troy, Alabama where he majored in Business Administration. He was chosen Gulf South Conference Freshmen of the Year in 1982 while playing nose guard, before finishing his college career as outside linebacker. Made All-Gulf South Conference Linebacker in 1984. During his four years at Troy he had 87 tackles, 118 assist, 11 sacks and 7 broken passes.<ref>http://www.datebasefootball.com{{dead link|date=October 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Professional career==
Henton was selected by the Pittsburgh Steelers in the ninth round of the [[1986 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1986 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1986/draft.htm |access-date=October 3, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> During his first season in Pittsburgh, he was voted as the Steelers Defensive Rookie of the Year and honored with the prestigious "Mean Joe Greene Award". He played two seasons for the Steelers at linebacker. In 1991, Henton was selected by the Sacramento Surge becoming the first pick in the first round for the World League Of American Football (WLAF). During the 1992 season, his former college coach, [[Chan Gailey]], went into negotiations with the Surge to bring Henton back home to Birmingham where he finished his career as a professional football player.<ref name="DBFbio"/>

'''Anthony Gaitor''' (born October 9, 1988) is an American former professional [[Gridiron football|football]] [[cornerback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL). He was selected by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in the seventh round of the [[2011 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] at [[FIU Panthers football|Florida International]].

==Early life==
A native of [[Miami]], Gaitor attended [[Miami Northwestern Senior High School|Miami Northwestern High School]], where he played on a squad that included other future NFL players: [[Lavonte David]], [[Marcus Forston]], [[Jacory Harris]], [[Tommy Streeter]], [[Sean Spence]], and [[Brandon Washington]]. Regarded as only a two-star recruit by [[Rivals.com]], Gaitor was not listed among the top cornerbacks of his class.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/player-Anthony-Gaitor-61616 |title=Anthony Gaitor - Yahoo! Sports |access-date=2014-04-19 |archive-date=2014-04-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140426095744/https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/player-Anthony-Gaitor-61616 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==College career==
Gaitor attended [[Florida International University]] from 2007 to 2010. In his career, he accumulated 197 total tackles, including 19 for loss, four sacks, 11 interceptions (three which he returned for touchdowns), and 35 passes defended.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anthony Gaitor College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/anthony-gaitor-1.html |access-date=2023-06-26 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

==Professional career==

===Tampa Bay Buccaneers (first stint)===
Gaitor was selected by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in the seventh round, 222nd overall, of the [[2011 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2011/draft.htm |title=2011 NFL Draft Listing |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2019-02-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.tampabay.com/blogs/bucs/content/bucs-select-fiu-cb-anthony-gaitor-seventh-round-222nd-overall |title=Bucs select FIU CB Anthony Gaitor in the seventh round, 222nd overall |access-date=2013-01-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120412065724/http://www.tampabay.com/blogs/bucs/content/bucs-select-fiu-cb-anthony-gaitor-seventh-round-222nd-overall |archive-date=2012-04-12 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Bucs select FIU CB Anthony Gaitor in the seventh round, 222nd overall | website=Tampa Bay Times | date=2011-05-03 | url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/2011/04/30/bucs-select-fiu-cb-anthony-gaitor-in-the-seventh-round-222nd-overall/ | access-date=2025-07-17}}</ref> On August 26, 2013, he was placed on injured-reserve, thus ending his 2013 season.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://bucsscene.blogs.theledger.com/14195/gaitor-smith-placed-on-injured-reserve-seasons-over/ |title=Gaitor, Smith Placed on injured reserve; Season's Over |access-date=2014-04-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413144732/http://bucsscene.blogs.theledger.com/14195/gaitor-smith-placed-on-injured-reserve-seasons-over/ |archive-date=2014-04-13 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Miami Dolphins===
Gaitor signed with the [[Miami Dolphins]] on May 28, 2014.

===Tampa Bay Buccaneers (second stint)===
On July 28, 2014, the Buccaneers re-signed Gaitor.<ref>
{{Cite web |url=http://www.nationalfootballpost.com/Buccaneers-resign-Anthony-Gaitor.html |title=Buccaneers re-sign Anthony Gaitor | National Football Post |access-date=2014-07-28 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20140806152534/http://www.nationalfootballpost.com/Buccaneers-resign-Anthony-Gaitor.html |archive-date=2014-08-06 |url-status=dead }}
</ref> The Buccaneers released Gaitor on August 29, 2014.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.buccaneers.com/news/article-smith/Bucs-Begin-Final-Cuts/061cd781-f737-4f21-813c-fe0d36c7b7b5 |title=Bucs Begin Final Cuts |access-date=2014-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140901150244/http://www.buccaneers.com/news/article-smith/Bucs-Begin-Final-Cuts/061cd781-f737-4f21-813c-fe0d36c7b7b5 |archive-date=2014-09-01 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Arizona Cardinals===
Gaitor signed with the [[Arizona Cardinals]] practice squad on August 31, 2014.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Allen|first1=Scott|title=CB Anthony Gaitor Added to Arizona Cardinals Practice Squad|date=31 August 2014|url=http://raisingzona.com/2014/08/31/cb-anthony-gaitor-added-arizona-cardinals-practice-squad/|publisher=raisingzona.com|access-date=4 September 2014}}</ref> On October 28, 2014, he was released from Arizona's practice squad.

===BC Lions (first stint)===
Gaitor signed with the [[BC Lions]] of the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) on February 25, 2016, and was released by the team on June 3, 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bclions.com/transactions/ |title=BC LIONS TRANSACTIONS |publisher=bclions.com |access-date=June 16, 2016 |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160617000810/http://www.bclions.com/transactions/ |archive-date=June 17, 2016 }}</ref> He was recalled July 24, 2016. Gaiter played in 11 games for the Lions in 2016, contributing 35 tackles, 2 interceptions, 1 forced fumble, and 1 defensive touchdown. He was released by the Lions on January 9, 2017, allowing him to pursue an NFL contract.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.tsn.ca/lions-grant-free-agent-status-to-gaitor-bazzie-1.646777|title=Lions grant free agent status to Gaitor, Bazzie – Article – TSN|date=2017-01-09|newspaper=TSN|access-date=2017-01-10}}</ref>

===New Orleans Saints===
Later that same day (January 9, 2017) Gaitor signed a reserve/future contract with the [[New Orleans Saints]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Saints sign CB Anthony Gaitor, third CFL player to join this week|url=http://www.nola.com/saints/index.ssf/2017/01/saints_sign_cb_anthony_gaitor.html|author=Katzenstein, Josh|website=NOLA.com|date=January 6, 2017}}</ref> He was waived by the Saints on May 15, 2017.<ref>{{cite web|title=Saints Announce Roster Moves After Rookie Minicamp|url=http://www.neworleanssaints.com/news-and-events/article-1/Saints-Announce-Roster-Moves-After-Rookie-Minicamp/bcb464d1-d42b-4f6b-b488-6525f760f657|website=NewOrleansSaints.com|date=May 15, 2017|access-date=May 16, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170517213729/http://www.neworleanssaints.com/news-and-events/article-1/Saints-Announce-Roster-Moves-After-Rookie-Minicamp/bcb464d1-d42b-4f6b-b488-6525f760f657|archive-date=May 17, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===BC Lions (second stint)===
Gaitor signed with the Lions on May 29, 2017.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bclions.com/2017/05/29/lions-bring-back-anthony-gaitor/ | title=LIONS BRING BACK ANTHONY GAITOR | publisher=bclions.com | date=May 29, 2017 | accessdate=May 24, 2024}}</ref>

===Winnipeg Blue Bombers===
Gaitor was signed by the [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]] on February 1, 2018.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bluebombers.com/2018/02/01/bombers-sign-defensive-back-anthony-gaitor/ | title=BOMBERS SIGN DEFENSIVE BACK ANTHONY GAITOR | publisher=bluebombers.com | date=February 1, 2018 | accessdate=May 24, 2024}}</ref> He left the team in November 2019 after refusing a role change.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://globalnews.ca/news/6142603/winnipeg-blue-bombers-anthony-gaitor/ | title=Winnipeg Blue Bombers split ways with Anthony Gaitor ahead of playoff game | publisher=globalnews.ca | date=November 7, 2019 | accessdate=May 24, 2024 | author=Hobson, Russ}}</ref>

==Coaching career==
Gaitor currently is a defensive quality control assistant for Florida International football. As of late March 2023, Gaitor was promoted to outside linebackers coach for Florida International. He currently serves as the cornerbacks coach at FIU.

'''Anthony Glenn Herron'''<ref name="marriage"/> (born September 24, 1979) is an American [[American football|football]] commentator and former [[defensive end]]. Originally from [[Bolingbrook, Illinois]], Herron played [[college football]] at [[Iowa Hawkeyes football|Iowa]]. Following the [[2001 NFL draft]], Herron signed with the [[Detroit Lions]] as an undrafted free agent and spent three seasons with the team, in addition to short stints with the [[Green Bay Packers]], [[Pittsburgh Steelers]], and [[Atlanta Falcons]]. Although Herron played in only one NFL game, he had a more productive career in the [[Arena Football League]] with the [[Indiana Firebirds]] in 2004 and [[Nashville Kats]] in 2006 and 2007. A regular starter for the Kats in 2006, Herron played a total of 26 games in the Arena Football League.

After his playing career, Herron was assistant head coach and defensive coordinator for the [[Tennessee Valley Vipers]] of [[af2]] from 2008 to 2009, helping the Vipers win the [[ArenaCup IX]] title in 2008. Herron also became a college football and NFL commentator on Chicago-area and national TV and radio, including the [[Big Ten Network]], [[Pac-12 Network]], and [[SiriusXM]].

==Early life and college career==
Born and raised in [[Bolingbrook, Illinois]], Herron graduated from [[Bolingbrook High School]] in 1997. He played football, basketball, and track in high school.<ref name="Iowa">{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20021120094656/http://www.hawkeyefootball.com/2000/players/99.htm|archivedate=November 20, 2002|title=Anthony Herron|url=http://www.hawkeyefootball.com/2000/players/99.htm|publisher=University of Iowa|work=HawkeyeFootball.com|accessdate=September 27, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref> At the [[University of Iowa]], Herron played at defensive end from 1997 to 2000 and was a regular starter in his last two seasons.<ref name="Iowa"/> As a senior in [[2000 Iowa Hawkeyes football team|2000]], Herron had an honorable mention [[List of All-Big Ten Conference football teams|All-Big Ten]] season after making 64 tackles, three sacks, and two forced fumbles.<ref name="Falcons">{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20051127233757/http://www.atlantafalcons.com:80/team/playerBio.jsp?id=1577|archivedate=November 27, 2005|title=Anthony Herron|url=http://www.atlantafalcons.com/team/playerBio.jsp?id=1577|publisher=Atlanta Falcons|accessdate=September 27, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref> In his college career, Herron had 172 tackles (including 19 for loss), 10 sacks, and one blocked kick.<ref name="Kats"/> Herron completed his bachelor's degree in English at [[Tennessee State University]] during the 2006 offseason while playing for the [[Nashville Kats]] of the [[Arena Football League]].<ref name="Kats"/>

==Pro football career==
===NFL===
After the [[2001 NFL draft]], Herron signed as an undrafted free agent with the [[2001 Detroit Lions season|Detroit Lions]] on April 27, 2001 and was released on September 2 following the preseason.<ref name="Falcons"/> On September 4, Herron signed with the [[2001 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]]. He was released on October 5 but re-signed with the Packers practice squad two weeks later on October 19.<ref name="Falcons"/> The Lions signed Herron to its active roster off the Packers practice squad on November 27.<ref name="Falcons"/> Herron made his NFL debut coming off the bench during the Lions' 2001 season finale, a 15–10 win over the [[2001 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]] on January 6, 2002 that also marked the last NFL game played at the [[Pontiac Silverdome]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/H/HerrAn21/gamelog/|title=Anthony Herron Career Game Log|publisher=Pro Football Reference|accessdate=September 27, 2020}}</ref><ref name="Falcons"/> That game would be Herron's only career game in the NFL.<ref>{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20050406104114/http://www.nfl.com/players/playerpage/236948|archivedate=April 6, 2005|title=Anthony Herron|publisher=NFL|url=https://www.nfl.com/players/anthony-herron/|accessdate=September 27, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Due to a foot injury, Herron was on the Lions' physically unable to perform list throughout the 2002 season. The Lions released Herron on August 26, 2003.<ref name="Falcons"/> In 2004, Herron signed with the [[2004 Pittsburgh Steelers season|Pittsburgh Steelers]] on August 9 but was cut on August 27. Later that  year, he signed with the [[2004 Atlanta Falcons season|Atlanta Falcons]] practice squad on November 10. He was released on December 14 but re-signed with the practice squad on January 5, 2005.<ref name="Falcons"/> Following the 2005 preseason, Herron was waived during final roster cuts on September 3.<ref>{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20051130054258/http://www.atlantafalcons.com/team/article.jsp?id=8119|archivedate=November 30, 2005|title=Falcons make 21 moves to reach 53-man roster limit|url=http://www.atlantafalcons.com/team/article.jsp?id=8119|date=September 3, 2005|publisher=Atlanta Falcons|accessdate=September 27, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Arena Football League===
In 2004, Herron played in eight games for the [[Indiana Firebirds]] of the [[Arena Football League]], recording 10 tackles, defending one pass, and making eight quarterback hurries.<ref name="ArenaFan"/><ref name="Kats">{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070624160321/http://www.katsonline.com/team/players/name.php?PRKey=19|archivedate=June 24, 2007|title=Anthony Herron|url=http://www.katsonline.com/team/players/name.php?PRKey=19|publisher=Nashville Kats|accessdate=September 27, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref> From 2006 to 2007, Herron played at both offensive and defensive line for the [[Nashville Kats]], wearing jersey #99. Starting 11 games in 2006 and playing four games off the bench in 2007, Herron had 20.5 total tackles and four sacks in two seasons.<ref name="ArenaFan">{{cite web|url=http://www.arenafan.com/players/Anthony_Herron-4360/|title=Anthony Herron|publisher=ArenaFan|accessdate=September 27, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Anthony Herron Game Logs for the 2007 Season |url=http://www.arenafan.com/players/?page=players&player=4360&pageview=gamelogs |publisher=ArenaFan |accessdate=September 27, 2020}}</ref> He had one seven-yard touchdown reception in 2006.<ref name="ArenaFan"/>

==Coaching career==
In 2008 and 2009, Herron was assistant head coach and defensive coordinator for the [[Alabama Vipers|Tennessee Valley Vipers]] of the Arena Football League's minor league [[af2]].<ref name="wings">{{cite web|url=https://www.thegazette.com/2009/08/20/former-hawkeye-herron-stretching-his-wings|title=Former Hawkeye Herron stretching his wings|last=Hlas|first=Mike|work=The Gazette|place=Cedar Rapids, Iowa|date=August 20, 2009|accessdate=September 27, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090817041815/http://blog.al.com/mccarter/2009/07/vipers_vs_green_bay_two_footba.html|archivedate=August 17, 2009|title=Vipers vs. Green Bay: Two football traditions|last=McCarter|first=Mark|work=McCarter's Musings|publisher=AL.com|date=July 30, 2009|url=https://www.al.com/mccarter/2009/07/vipers_vs_green_bay_two_footba.html|accessdate=September 27, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref> He helped the Vipers win the [[ArenaCup IX]] title.<ref name="Football U">{{cite web|url=https://footballuniversity.org/coach/anthony-herron/|title=Anthony Herron|publisher=Football University|accessdate=September 27, 2020}}</ref>

==Broadcasting career==
Herron has worked for the [[Big Ten Network]] as a game and studio analyst, [[NFL Network]] as an analyst for Arena Football, and [[NBC Sports]] as a college football analyst.<ref name="Football U"/> Since 2013, he has been a college football analyst for the [[Pac-12 Network]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Mast|first=Allison|url=https://pac-12.com/news/2015/9/5/veteran-analyst-anthony-herron-shines-rookie-debut-studio-host.aspx|title=Veteran analyst Anthony Herron shines in rookie debut as studio host|publisher=Pac-12 Network|date=September 5, 2015|access-date=September 27, 2020}}</ref> Herron is a college football commentator for Chicago sports radio station [[WSCR]] "670 the Score" and Chicago Bears commentator for Chicago TV station [[WFLD]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.radio.com/670thescore/anthony-herron-iowa-hawkeyes-chris-doyle-racism-allegations-kirk-ferentz-knew-some-culture|title=Herron: I Accept Ferentz Missed Extent Of Allegations|publisher=670 the Score|accessdate=September 27, 2020|date=June 8, 2020}}</ref> In addition, he is also a host for the [[SiriusXM]] Big Ten Radio channel.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.siriusxm.com/siriusxmbigtenradio|title = SiriusXM Big Ten Radio}}</ref>

==Personal life==
In 2003, Herron married Katherine Druley in [[East Falmouth, Massachusetts]].<ref name="marriage">{{cite web|url=https://www.capecodtimes.com/article/20030914/LIFE0901/309149951|title=Herron-Druley|work=Cape Cod Times|date=September 14, 2003|accessdate=September 27, 2020}}</ref> He lived in [[Dearborn, Michigan]] while playing for the Lions.<ref name="marriage"/>

'''Anthony Johnson''' (born January 24, 1993) is an American former professional [[Gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[LSU Tigers football|LSU Tigers]]. During his [[high school football]] career at [[O. Perry Walker High School]] in [[New Orleans]], Johnson broke the Louisiana career [[quarterback sack|sack]] record with 67.5.

== Early life ==
Born to Nakisha Johnson and Sherman Patty and raised in [[New Orleans]], Johnson's family was displaced by [[Hurricane Katrina]] in 2005, and moved to [[Atlanta]], and later [[Mobile, Alabama]], for a period of time.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://theadvocate.com/football/6763566-175/anthony-the-freak-johnson-is |title=Music came first for LSU's vocal leader: Anthony 'The Freak' Johnson |date=August 28, 2013 |work=The Advocate }}</ref>

After returning to New Orleans, Johnson attended [[O. Perry Walker High School]], where he was a four-time all-district selection. He broke the Louisiana career sack record with 67.5 sacks during his four-year career. As a senior in 2010, he recorded 129 tackles, 31 tackles for loss, and 17.5 sacks. The team went 9–4 on the season, advancing to the LHSAA Class 4A semifinals, where they lost 36–6 to [[Franklinton High School (Louisiana)|Franklinton]]. Both ''[[USA Today]]'' and ''[[Parade (magazine)|Parade]]'' named Johnson to their All-American teams. [[Gatorade]] named him the Louisiana State Player of the Year, as the first lineman, and only third defender, in the 16 years of the award.

One of the most sought after high school players in the country, Johnson was rated as a five-star prospect by every recruiting service. [[Rivals.com]] ranked him the No. 1 defensive tackle of his class,<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/rankings/rank-2660 |title=Archived copy |access-date=March 7, 2015 |archive-date=March 5, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305064057/https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/rankings/rank-2660 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and compared him to [[Darnell Dockett]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/footballrecruiting/football/recruiting/player-Anthony-Johnson-79041 |title=Anthony Johnson - Yahoo! Sports |access-date=March 7, 2015 |archive-date=April 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402122124/https://sports.yahoo.com/footballrecruiting/football/recruiting/player-Anthony-Johnson-79041 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Johnson chose LSU over offers from almost every major school, including [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama]], [[Oklahoma Sooners football|Oklahoma]], and [[USC Trojans football|Southern California]].

== College career ==

Johnson played in thirteen games for LSU in 2011, and was named to both the [[CBSSports.com]] and Sporting News Freshman All-American teams.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://eye-on-collegefootball.blogs.cbssports.com/mcc/blogs/entry/24156338/33745625 |title=CBSSports.com 2011 Freshman All-America team - CBSSports.com |access-date=December 29, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120107161448/http://eye-on-collegefootball.blogs.cbssports.com/mcc/blogs/entry/24156338/33745625 |archive-date=January 7, 2012 }}</ref> He was named full-time starter in his junior year for the 2013 football season. Johnson declared for the [[2014 NFL draft]] after his junior season.<ref>[http://www.shreveporttimes.com/article/20140103/SPORTS0202/140103016/LSU-s-Ego-Ferguson-Anthony-Johnson-enter-NFL-Draft LSU's Ego Ferguson and Anthony Johnson to enter NFL Draft]</ref>

The [[Washington Redskins]] signed Johnson to their practice squad on November 9, 2015.<ref>{{cite web|work=Redskins.com|url=http://www.redskins.com/news-and-events/blog/article-1/More-On-The-Redskins-Three-New-Roster-Additions/573f4ca0-c1f6-45b8-8c60-f1a8de50d0a1|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160917184539/http://www.redskins.com/news-and-events/blog/article-1/More-On-The-Redskins-Three-New-Roster-Additions/573f4ca0-c1f6-45b8-8c60-f1a8de50d0a1|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 17, 2016|title= More On The Redskins' Three New Roster Additions|first=Jake|last=Kring-Schreifels|date=November 9, 2015|access-date=November 9, 2015}}</ref>

On September 1, 2018, Johnson was placed on injured reserve.<ref>{{cite web|title=Colts Announce Final 2018 Roster Cuts|url=https://www.colts.com/news/colts-announce-final-2018-roster-cuts|author=Walker, Andrew|website=Colts.com|date=September 1, 2018}}</ref> He was released by Indianapolis on September 11.
